The minimum description length (MDL) principle suggests that if the description length of the world model is substantially smaller than that of the policy, using LLM as a world model for planning is likely better than using it solely as a policy.
In object rearrangement, LLM-MCTS effectively combines the LLM as a world model and as a heuristic policy to overcome the limitations of each individual approach.
The performance of LLM as a policy degrades quickly for novel, complex tasks, while LLM-MCTS maintains robust performance.
papers.limitation:
The MDL analysis assumes iid data and may not hold in practice, and error propagation may need separate analysis.
Policy errors (e.g., generating inadmissible actions), model errors (incorrect object position predictions), and translation errors (mapping LLM outputs to admissible actions) can lead to task failures.
papers.abstract: Large-scale task planning is a major challenge. Recent work exploits large language models (LLMs) directly as a policy and shows surprisingly interesting results. This paper shows that LLMs provide a commonsense model of the world in addition to a policy that acts on it. The world model and the policy can be combined in a search algorithm, such as Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS), to scale up task planning. In our new LLM-MCTS algorithm, the LLM-induced world model provides a commonsense prior belief for MCTS to achieve effective reasoning; the LLM-induced policy acts as a heuristic to guide the search, vastly improving search efficiency. Experiments show that LLM-MCTS outperforms both MCTS alone and policies induced by LLMs (GPT2 and GPT3.5) by a wide margin, for complex, novel tasks. Further experiments and analyses on multiple tasks -- multiplication, multi-hop travel planning, object rearrangement -- suggest minimum description length (MDL) as a general guiding principle: if the description length of the world model is substantially smaller than that of the policy, using LLM as a world model for model-based planning is likely better than using LLM solely as a policy.

papers.title: What shapes feature representations? Exploring datasets, architectures, and training
papers.research_question: What features do models use and represent when there are multiple task-relevant or irrelevant features, and how do inductive biases and training affect this?
papers.core_contribution: Models preferentially represent features that are more decodable from the untrained model, enhancing task-relevant features and suppressing irrelevant ones, and sometimes suppress more predictive but harder features in favor of easier ones.
papers.conclusion: Model representations are shaped by inductive biases and training; practitioners should not assume label-relevant features are used; analyzing untrained models can predict feature usage; representational similarity analyses should be interpreted with care.
papers.key_findings:
Many input features are partially represented in untrained models.
Training enhances task-relevant features and suppresses task-irrelevant features.
When two features redundantly predict the label, models prefer the one more decodable from the untrained model.
An easier, weakly predictive feature can suppress a more strongly predictive but harder feature.
Easy features lead to more consistent representations across model runs than hard features, and multi-task models resemble those trained only on the easy feature.
papers.limitation: The results are shown across multiple architectures and datasets but may not generalize to broader settings.
future_direction: Explore broader settings beyond the architectures and datasets studied.
Investigate the effect of fully-connected layer width on feature representations.
papers.abstract: In naturalistic learning problems, a model's input contains a wide range of features, some useful for the task at hand, and others not. Of the useful features, which ones does the model use? Of the task-irrelevant features, which ones does the model represent? Answers to these questions are important for understanding the basis of models' decisions, as well as for building models that learn versatile, adaptable representations useful beyond the original training task. We study these questions using synthetic datasets in which the task-relevance of input features can be controlled directly. We find that when two features redundantly predict the labels, the model preferentially represents one, and its preference reflects what was most linearly decodable from the untrained model. Over training, task-relevant features are enhanced, and task-irrelevant features are partially suppressed. Interestingly, in some cases, an easier, weakly predictive feature can suppress a more strongly predictive, but more difficult one. Additionally, models trained to recognize both easy and hard features learn representations most similar to models that use only the easy feature. Further, easy features lead to more consistent representations across model runs than do hard features. Finally, models have greater representational similarity to an untrained model than to models trained on a different task. Our results highlight the complex processes that determine which features a model represents.

papers.title: How Do Large Language Models Learn Concepts During Continual Pre-Training?
papers.research_question: How do large language models acquire, retain, and forget concepts during continual pretraining? Specifically, how do internal concept representations correlate with concept acquisition and forgetting, and how do they relate to interference and synergy among multiple concepts and knowledge types during joint training?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces a circuit-level analysis of concept learning in LLMs during continual pre-training, revealing that concept circuits provide signals for learning and forgetting dynamics, and show patterns like stage-wise temporal changes and interference/synergy effects.
papers.conclusion: The work offers a circuit-level view of concept learning dynamics and informs the design of more interpretable and robust concept-aware training strategies for LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Concept circuits provide a non-trivial, statistically significant signal of concept learning and forgetting.
Concept circuits exhibit a stage-wise temporal pattern during continual pretraining, with an early increase followed by gradual decrease and stabilization.
Concepts with larger learning gains tend to exhibit greater forgetting under subsequent training.
Semantically similar concepts induce stronger interference than weakly related ones.
Conceptual knowledge differs in transferability, with some significantly facilitating the learning of others.
papers.limitation:
Limited model scale, focusing only on GPT-2 Large and LLaMA-3.2-1B, not larger models.
Exploration of actionable training strategies is left for future work.
future_direction: Extending analysis to larger-scale models.
Exploring circuit-aware training effort allocation and interference-aware data scheduling.
papers.abstract: Human beings primarily understand the world through concepts (e.g., dog), abstract mental representations that structure perception, reasoning, and learning. However, how large language models (LLMs) acquire, retain, and forget such concepts during continual pretraining remains poorly understood. In this work, we study how individual concepts are acquired and forgotten, as well as how multiple concepts interact through interference and synergy. We link these behavioral dynamics to LLMs' internal Concept Circuits, computational subgraphs associated with specific concepts, and incorporate Graph Metrics to characterize circuit structure. Our analysis reveals: (1) LLMs concept circuits provide a non-trivial, statistically significant signal of concept learning and forgetting; (2) Concept circuits exhibit a stage-wise temporal pattern during continual pretraining, with an early increase followed by gradual decrease and stabilization; (3) concepts with larger learning gains tend to exhibit greater forgetting under subsequent training; (4) semantically similar concepts induce stronger interference than weakly related ones; (5) conceptual knowledge differs in their transferability, with some significantly facilitating the learning of others. Together, our findings offer a circuit-level view of concept learning dynamics and inform the design of more interpretable and robust concept-aware training strategies for LLMs.

papers.title: Towards Tracing Knowledge in Language Models Back to the Training Data
papers.research_question: How can we identify which training examples taught a language model to generate a particular factual assertion?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the problem of fact tracing and presents the first quantitative benchmark (FTRACE) to evaluate training data attribution methods for tracing factual knowledge in language models back to specific training examples.
papers.conclusion: Significant headroom remains for improving training data attribution methods for fact tracing, with key challenges including gradient saturation and the importance of nuanced implementation details.
papers.key_findings:
Current TDA methods (gradient-based TRACIN and embedding-based EMBED) underperform a simple IR baseline (BM25) on the natural fact tracing benchmark (FTRACE-TREx).
On the controlled synthetic benchmark (FTRACE-SYNTH), TDA methods show better upper bounds, indicating potential when lexical overlap is reduced.
Optimizing TDA hyperparameters (e.g., layer selection, gradient normalization, using optimizer accumulators) significantly improves performance.
The embedding layer provides the most reliable attribution signal for both gradient and embedding-based methods.
Gradient saturation is a key challenge for TDA methods when facts are already known by the model.
papers.limitation:
Gradient saturation: when a model already knows a fact, gradients are near zero, making it difficult for TDA methods to attribute.
The natural benchmark (FTRACE-TREx) may have lexical overlap that favors surface-level IR methods like BM25.
future_direction: Improving TDA methods to overcome the gradient saturation problem.
Better handling of indirect proponents (facts inferred from other facts).
papers.abstract: Language models (LMs) have been shown to memorize a great deal of factual knowledge contained in their training data. But when an LM generates an assertion, it is often difficult to determine where it learned this information and whether it is true. In this paper, we propose the problem of fact tracing: identifying which training examples taught an LM to generate a particular factual assertion. Prior work on training data attribution (TDA) may offer effective tools for identifying such examples, known as “proponents”. We present the first quantitative benchmark to evaluate this. We compare two popular families of TDA methods — gradient-based and embedding-based — and find that much headroom remains. For example, both methods have lower proponent-retrieval precision than an information retrieval baseline (BM25) that does not have access to the LM at all. We identify key challenges that may be necessary for further improvement such as overcoming the problem of gradient saturation, and also show how several nuanced implementation details of existing neural TDA methods can significantly improve overall fact tracing performance.

papers.title: Language Models Represent Space and Time
papers.research_question: Do large language models learn coherent linear representations of space and time, i.e., do they form a world model?
papers.core_contribution: Large language models learn linear representations of space and time that are robust to prompting and unified across entity types, and individual 'space' and 'time' neurons exist that encode these coordinates.
papers.conclusion: Modern LLMs learn rich spatiotemporal representations of the real world and possess basic ingredients of a world model.
papers.key_findings:
Linear probes can recover spatial and temporal coordinates from internal activations, with performance increasing with model size and plateauing in middle layers.
Spatial and temporal features are linearly represented, as nonlinear probes do not improve performance.
Representations are robust to variations in prompting, though random tokens or capitalization degrade performance.
Probes generalize across entity types and to held-out geographic or temporal blocks, indicating unified representations.
Individual neurons exist that are highly predictive of space and time, and causal interventions confirm their importance.
papers.limitation:
Data comes only from English Wikipedia, skewing towards the Anglosphere, and entity type distribution is not uniform.
The true extent and structure of spatial and temporal representations remain unclear.
future_direction: Extracting representations in the model’s coordinate system rather than human coordinates, e.g., with sparse autoencoders.
Studying how these spatiotemporal representations are learned, recalled, and used internally across training checkpoints.
Investigating potential parallels with biological place and grid cells in the brain.
papers.abstract: The capabilities of large language models (LLMs) have sparked debate over whether such systems just learn an enormous collection of superficial statistics or a set of more coherent and grounded representations that reflect the real world. We find evidence for the latter by analyzing the learned representations of three spatial datasets (world, US, NYC places) and three temporal datasets (historical figures, artworks, news headlines) in the Llama-2 family of models. We discover that LLMs learn linear representations of space and time across multiple scales. These representations are robust to prompting variations and unified across different entity types (e.g. cities and landmarks). In addition, we identify individual "space neurons" and "time neurons" that reliably encode spatial and temporal coordinates. While further investigation is needed, our results suggest modern LLMs learn rich spatiotemporal representations of the real world and possess basic ingredients of a world model.

papers.title: When Do You Need Billions of Words of Pretraining Data?
papers.research_question: What knowledge or skills do Transformer LMs learn from large-scale pretraining that they cannot learn from less data, and how much pretraining data is required to learn different linguistic features?
papers.core_contribution: Linguistic features are learned with relatively little pretraining data (10M-100M words), while commonsense knowledge and downstream NLU task performance require billions of words.
papers.conclusion: Linguistic features are mostly learnable with 100M words of data, while NLU task performance requires far more data, suggesting that other forms of knowledge (e.g., commonsense) are the major drivers of improvements in large pretrained models.
papers.key_findings:
Linguistic features (syntactic and semantic) are mostly learnable with 100M words of pretraining data.
Commonsense knowledge, as measured by the Winograd task, requires more data and improves up to 30B words.
Performance on NLU tasks (SuperGLUE) requires billions of words and does not saturate at 30B words.
There is variation in data needs for different linguistic phenomena: agreement phenomena are learned quickly, while wh-dependencies and quantifiers require more data or are not learned effectively.
The accessibility of features, as measured by minimum description length probing, does not show a different trend from classifier probing.
papers.limitation:
The Winograd task results are somewhat noisy due to well-known idiosyncrasies of the task.
The MDL method may not adequately differentiate between feature information and accessibility, as the overall codelength predominantly reflects the decrease in loss.
The experiments focus mainly on linguistic knowledge, so additional work is needed to give a more complete picture of the acquisition of commonsense knowledge.
future_direction: Use causal probing methods like amnesic probing to understand what causes NLU task performance to improve with large quantities of data.
Understand the differences between learning curves for various linguistic features, e.g., whether some features acquired earlier bootstrap knowledge of other features.
Extend the investigation to other pretraining settings, model architectures, pretraining tasks, and data domains to close the gap between models and human learners.
papers.abstract: NLP is currently dominated by general-purpose pretrained language models like RoBERTa, which achieve strong performance on NLU tasks through pretraining on billions of words. But what exact knowledge or skills do Transformer LMs learn from large-scale pretraining that they cannot learn from less data? We adopt four probing methods---classifier probing, information-theoretic probing, unsupervised relative acceptability judgment, and fine-tuning on NLU tasks---and draw learning curves that track the growth of these different measures of linguistic ability with respect to pretraining data volume using the MiniBERTas, a group of RoBERTa models pretrained on 1M, 10M, 100M and 1B words. We find that LMs require only about 10M or 100M words to learn representations that reliably encode most syntactic and semantic features we test. A much larger quantity of data is needed in order to acquire enough commonsense knowledge and other skills required to master typical downstream NLU tasks. The results suggest that, while the ability to encode linguistic features is almost certainly necessary for language understanding, it is likely that other forms of knowledge are the major drivers of recent improvements in language understanding among large pretrained models.

papers.title: On the relationship between class selectivity, dimensionality, and robustness
papers.research_question: Does class selectivity confer robustness or vulnerability to input perturbations, and what is the underlying mechanism?
papers.core_contribution: Class selectivity causally affects robustness: lower selectivity improves robustness to naturalistic corruptions but increases vulnerability to adversarial attacks, mediated by changes in representational dimensionality and stability.
papers.conclusion: Class selectivity mediates a trade-off between robustness to naturalistic corruptions and adversarial attacks, with low selectivity improving corruption robustness but increasing adversarial vulnerability, and this is reflected in the dimensionality of activations and network stability.
papers.key_findings:
Decreasing class selectivity decreases vulnerability to naturalistic corruptions.
Decreasing class selectivity increases vulnerability to gradient-based adversarial attacks.
The dimensionality of activation changes due to perturbation is higher for low-selectivity networks, especially for adversarial attacks.
The input-output Jacobian (stability) is inversely proportional to class selectivity, explaining adversarial vulnerability.
There is a trade-off between robustness to naturalistic and adversarial perturbations mediated by class selectivity and dimensionality.
papers.limitation: Tiny ImageNetC may be out-of-distribution relative to Tiny ImageNet training data, potentially underestimating corruption robustness.
papers.abstract: While the relative trade-offs between sparse and distributed representations in deep neural networks (DNNs) are well-studied, less is known about how these trade-offs apply to representations of semantically-meaningful information. Class selectivity, the variability of a unit's responses across data classes or dimensions, is one way of quantifying the sparsity of semantic representations. Given recent evidence showing that class selectivity can impair generalization, we sought to investigate whether it also confers robustness (or vulnerability) to perturbations of input data. We found that mean class selectivity predicts vulnerability to naturalistic corruptions; networks regularized to have lower levels of class selectivity are more robust to corruption, while networks with higher class selectivity are more vulnerable to corruption, as measured using Tiny ImageNetC and CIFAR10C. In contrast, we found that class selectivity increases robustness to multiple types of gradient-based adversarial attacks. To examine this difference, we studied the dimensionality of the change in the representation due to perturbation, finding that decreasing class selectivity increases the dimensionality of this change for both corruption types, but with a notably larger increase for adversarial attacks. These results demonstrate the causal relationship between selectivity and robustness and provide new insights into the mechanisms of this relationship.

papers.title: Triple Phase Transitions: Understanding the Learning Dynamics of Large Language Models from a Neuroscience Perspective
papers.research_question: How do phase transitions in large language model training manifest in terms of alignment with human brain activity, internal representations, and downstream task performance?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies three common phase transitions in LLM training: an initial alignment with the brain when instruction following emerges, a detachment during task performance stagnation, and a realignment when tasks are consolidated.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates that LLM learning involves three phase transitions that synchronize brain alignment, internal representations, and task performance, providing a multi-scale view of emergent abilities.
papers.key_findings:
Phase 1 (Brain Alignment and Instruction Following): Alignment with the entire brain surges as LLMs begin adhering to task instructions.
Phase 2 (Brain Detachment and Stagnation): LLMs diverge from the brain during a period of downstream task accuracy stagnation.
Phase 3 (Brain Realignment and Consolidation): Alignment with the brain reoccurs as LLMs become capable of solving downstream tasks.
These three phase transitions are observed across LLMs with distinct architectures and training data.
The transitions only occur when the input language matches a language sufficiently represented in the model's training corpus.
papers.limitation: The brain encoding accuracy and intrinsic dimensionality are not perfectly congruent, leaving open questions about what aspects of activation changes are not captured by intrinsic dimensionality alone.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) often exhibit abrupt emergent behavior, whereby new abilities arise at certain points during their training. This phenomenon, commonly referred to as a ''phase transition'', remains poorly understood. In this study, we conduct an integrative analysis of such phase transitions by examining three interconnected perspectives: the similarity between LLMs and the human brain, the internal states of LLMs, and downstream task performance. We propose a novel interpretation for the learning dynamics of LLMs that vary in both training data and architecture, revealing that three phase transitions commonly emerge across these models during training: (1) alignment with the entire brain surges as LLMs begin adhering to task instructions Brain Alignment and Instruction Following, (2) unexpectedly, LLMs diverge from the brain during a period in which downstream task accuracy temporarily stagnates Brain Detachment and Stagnation, and (3) alignment with the brain reoccurs as LLMs become capable of solving the downstream tasks Brain Realignment and Consolidation. These findings illuminate the underlying mechanisms of phase transitions in LLMs, while opening new avenues for interdisciplinary research bridging AI and neuroscience.

papers.title: Entities as Experts: Sparse Memory Access with Entity Supervision
papers.research_question: How can we develop neural sequence models that capture knowledge about real-world entities by learning entity representations directly from text, enabling sparse memory access?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Entities as Experts (EAE), a transformer-based model that learns entity representations directly from text and accesses them sparsely via an entity memory layer, demonstrating improved performance on knowledge probing and question answering tasks compared to larger models.
papers.conclusion: EAE effectively captures declarative knowledge in entity representations and outperforms larger models on knowledge-intensive tasks, but it cannot handle unseen entities and future work should explore representations for rare entities and integration with knowledge bases.
papers.key_findings:
EAE outperforms larger models like BERT-large and T5-3B on TriviaQA and LAMA knowledge probes.
Supervision via entity linking is crucial for the entity memory layer's performance; unsupervised memory access performs worse.
EAE's learned entity representations are more effective than pre-trained embeddings from KNOWBERT and ERNIE on knowledge probing tasks.
Sparse access (retrieving top-k entity memories) works effectively with little performance drop, enabling efficient inference.
Correct identification and linking of entity mentions in questions is essential for EAE's question answering performance.
papers.limitation:
Cannot handle unseen entities due to fixed entity vocabulary.
Poor performance on non-entity concepts such as dates and common nouns.
future_direction: Explore representations for rare or unseen entities.
Develop less memory-intensive ways to learn and integrate entity representations.
Integrate information from external knowledge bases to improve entity representations.
papers.abstract: We focus on the problem of capturing declarative knowledge about entities in the learned parameters of a language model. We introduce a new model-Entities as Experts (EAE)that can access distinct memories of the entities mentioned in a piece of text. Unlike previous efforts to integrate entity knowledge into sequence models, EAE's entity representations are learned directly from text. We show that EAE's learned representations capture sufficient knowledge to answer TriviaQA questions such as "Which Dr. Who villain has been played by Roger Delgado, Anthony Ainley, Eric Roberts?", outperforming an encodergenerator Transformer model with 10 the parameters. According to the LAMA knowledge probes, EAE contains more factual knowledge than a similarly sized BERT, as well as previous approaches that integrate external sources of entity knowledge. Because EAE associates parameters with specific entities, it only needs to access a fraction of its parameters at inference time, and we show that the correct identification and representation of entities is essential to EAE's performance.

papers.title: Not All Neural Embeddings are Born Equal
papers.research_question: How does the architecture/objective function of neural models affect the information encoded in their word embeddings, specifically comparing translation-based and monolingual embeddings?
papers.core_contribution: Translation-based word embeddings outperform monolingual embeddings on tasks requiring knowledge of conceptual similarity and syntactic role, suggesting the translation objective better captures the ontological status of concepts.
papers.conclusion: Neural machine translation models learn word embeddings that more effectively encode conceptual similarity and syntactic role information compared to monolingual models, likely due to the cross-lingual alignment pressure of the translation objective.
papers.key_findings:
Translation-based embeddings achieve higher correlation on SimLex-999 (similarity) and higher accuracy on the TOEFL synonym test and synonym/antonym classification compared to monolingual embeddings.
Monolingual embeddings perform better on relatedness tasks (WordSim-353, MEN).
Translation-based embeddings excel at syntactic analogies, while monolingual embeddings are better at semantic analogies.
The performance advantage of translation-based embeddings on similarity tasks is not due to training data quantity, as monolingual models trained on larger corpora do not match their performance.
The translation objective may induce embeddings that better approximate ontological similarity by aligning words across languages, even when their co-occurrence patterns differ.
papers.abstract: Neural language models learn word representations that capture rich linguistic and conceptual information. Here we investigate the embeddings learned by neural machine translation models. We show that translation-based embeddings outperform those learned by cutting-edge monolingual models at single-language tasks requiring knowledge of conceptual similarity and/or syntactic role. The findings suggest that, while monolingual models learn information about how concepts are related, neural-translation models better capture their true ontological status.

papers.title: Learning Inductive Biases with Simple Neural Networks
papers.research_question: How do simple neural networks develop inductive biases like the shape bias, and under what conditions? How does the acquisition of this bias relate to vocabulary acceleration, mirroring child development?
papers.core_contribution: Simple neural networks can learn a shape bias from very few examples, and the development of this bias predicts vocabulary acceleration in the networks, consistent with developmental processes in children.
papers.conclusion: Neural networks can learn inductive biases like the shape bias from limited data, and the dynamics of this learning mirror child development, suggesting a connection between artificial and human learning.
papers.key_findings:
Multilayer perceptrons develop a shape bias after seeing as few as 3 examples of 4 object categories using abstract bit-vector patterns.
Convolutional neural networks develop a shape bias with as few as 6 examples of 8 object categories using synthetic images.
Networks show greater sensitivity to changes in shape than color after shape bias training, as shown by parametric manipulation of stimuli.
The development of the shape bias in CNNs correlates with the onset of vocabulary acceleration, mirroring the correlation observed in children.
Color bias training requires less data than shape bias training and does not follow the same two-step generalization process.
future_direction: Investigate the hypothesis of initializing large-scale image recognition models with shape bias training using ImageNet-scale DNNs.
papers.abstract: People use rich prior knowledge about the world in order to efficiently learn new concepts. These priors - also known as "inductive biases" - pertain to the space of internal models considered by a learner, and they help the learner make inferences that go beyond the observed data. A recent study found that deep neural networks optimized for object recognition develop the shape bias (Ritter et al., 2017), an inductive bias possessed by children that plays an important role in early word learning. However, these networks use unrealistically large quantities of training data, and the conditions required for these biases to develop are not well understood. Moreover, it is unclear how the learning dynamics of these networks relate to developmental processes in childhood. We investigate the development and influence of the shape bias in neural networks using controlled datasets of abstract patterns and synthetic images, allowing us to systematically vary the quantity and form of the experience provided to the learning algorithms. We find that simple neural networks develop a shape bias after seeing as few as 3 examples of 4 object categories. The development of these biases predicts the onset of vocabulary acceleration in our networks, consistent with the developmental process in children.

papers.title: On Linear Representations and Pretraining Data Frequency in Language Models
papers.research_question: What is the connection between pretraining data frequency and the formation of linear representations of factual relations in language models?
papers.core_contribution: The formation of linear representations for factual recall in language models is strongly correlated with pretraining term frequencies, and measuring these representations allows prediction of term frequencies in the pretraining corpus.
papers.conclusion: Linear representations of factual triplets in LMs are connected to pretraining frequencies, which can guide interpretability work and enable prediction of term frequencies in closed-data models.
papers.key_findings:
The development of linear representations for factual recall relations in LMs is related to frequency as well as model size.
Linear representations form at predictable frequency thresholds during training, regardless of when this threshold is met, and correlate strongly with recall accuracy.
Measuring the extent to which a relation is represented linearly allows prediction of the approximate frequencies of individual terms in the pretraining corpus, even without access to the training data.
The predictive signal from linear representations is stronger than that from log probabilities and task accuracies alone.
papers.limitation:
The study focuses on factual relations and leaves non-factual relations (e.g., gender stereotypes) for future work.
The regression model provides approximate frequency predictions within bounds, not exact counts.
future_direction: Extend the analysis to non-factual relations.
Improve the bounds of predicted frequencies.
Understand if and when LMs use non-linear methods to solve tasks.
papers.abstract: Pretraining data has a direct impact on the behaviors and quality of language models (LMs), but we only understand the most basic principles of this relationship. While most work focuses on pretraining data's effect on downstream task behavior, we investigate its relationship to LM representations. Previous work has discovered that, in language models, some concepts are encoded `linearly' in the representations, but what factors cause these representations to form? We study the connection between pretraining data frequency and models' linear representations of factual relations. We find evidence that the formation of linear representations is strongly connected to pretraining term frequencies; specifically for subject-relation-object fact triplets, both subject-object co-occurrence frequency and in-context learning accuracy for the relation are highly correlated with linear representations. This is the case across all phases of pretraining. In OLMo-7B and GPT-J, we discover that a linear representation consistently (but not exclusively) forms when the subjects and objects within a relation co-occur at least 1k and 2k times, respectively, regardless of when these occurrences happen during pretraining. Finally, we train a regression model on measurements of linear representation quality in fully-trained LMs that can predict how often a term was seen in pretraining. Our model achieves low error even on inputs from a different model with a different pretraining dataset, providing a new method for estimating properties of the otherwise-unknown training data of closed-data models. We conclude that the strength of linear representations in LMs contains signal about the models' pretraining corpora that may provide new avenues for controlling and improving model behavior: particularly, manipulating the models' training data to meet specific frequency thresholds.

papers.title: A Review of Developmental Interpretability in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: What is developmental interpretability, and how does it help understand the formation and evolution of capabilities in Large Language Models during training?
papers.core_contribution: This review synthesizes the field of developmental interpretability for LLMs, highlighting how understanding training dynamics can provide insights into capability formation and enhance AI safety.
papers.conclusion: Developmental interpretability reveals LLMs as dynamic systems with rich ontogeny, providing a proactive approach to AI safety by understanding capability formation during training.
papers.key_findings:
Induction heads form through composition of attention heads, enabling in-context learning.
Knowledge acquisition follows a biphasic pattern from formation to optimization.
Emergent abilities arise as phase transitions when pre-training loss crosses critical thresholds.
In-context learning can be transient and replaced by in-weights learning during overtraining.
Grokking involves delayed generalization after memorization.
papers.limitation:
Coverage limitations remain significant across current methodologies.
Feature ontology challenges include poorly defined concepts of what constitutes a 'feature'.
future_direction: Developing a unified theory of developmental dynamics
Creating robust benchmarks and metrics for interpretability
Expanding interpretability to multimodal and agentic AI systems
papers.abstract: This review synthesizes the nascent but critical field of developmental interpretability for Large Language Models. We chart the field's evolution from static, post-hoc analysis of trained models to a dynamic investigation of the training process itself. We begin by surveying the foundational methodologies, including representational probing, causal tracing, and circuit analysis, that enable researchers to deconstruct the learning process. The core of this review examines the developmental arc of LLM capabilities, detailing key findings on the formation and composition of computational circuits, the biphasic nature of knowledge acquisition, the transient dynamics of learning strategies like in-context learning, and the phenomenon of emergent abilities as phase transitions in training. We explore illuminating parallels with human cognitive and linguistic development, which provide valuable conceptual frameworks for understanding LLM learning. Finally, we argue that this developmental perspective is not merely an academic exercise but a cornerstone of proactive AI safety, offering a pathway to predict, monitor, and align the processes by which models acquire their capabilities. We conclude by outlining the grand challenges facing the field, such as scalability and automation, and propose a research agenda for building more transparent, reliable, and beneficial AI systems.

papers.title: Inference-Time Intervention: Eliciting Truthful Answers from a Language Model
papers.research_question: How can we enhance the truthfulness of large language models by intervening on their activations during inference?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Inference-Time Intervention (ITI), a minimally invasive technique that shifts activations along truthful directions in attention heads during inference to improve model truthfulness.
papers.conclusion: ITI is a promising, efficient method for improving truthfulness in LLMs, suggesting that models internally represent truth which can be elicited through activation shifts.
papers.key_findings:
ITI significantly improves truthfulness on the TruthfulQA benchmark, e.g., increasing Alpaca's truthfulness from 32.5% to 65.1%.
There is a trade-off between truthfulness and helpfulness that can be balanced by tuning intervention strength.
ITI is data-efficient, requiring only a few hundred examples to find truthful directions.
ITI generalizes to other question-answering benchmarks (Natural Questions, TriviaQA, MMLU) with smaller improvements.
LLMs appear to have an internal representation of truth even when generating falsehoods.
papers.limitation:
ITI is not sufficient for ensuring truthful answers from LLMs and should be part of a more comprehensive approach.
There is a trade-off between truthfulness and helpfulness; increasing truthfulness may reduce informativeness.
future_direction: Test ITI on a wider variety of benchmarks beyond TruthfulQA.
Investigate the mechanistic understanding of what ITI does to internal representations.
papers.abstract: We introduce Inference-Time Intervention (ITI), a technique designed to enhance the "truthfulness" of large language models (LLMs). ITI operates by shifting model activations during inference, following a set of directions across a limited number of attention heads. This intervention significantly improves the performance of LLaMA models on the TruthfulQA benchmark. On an instruction-finetuned LLaMA called Alpaca, ITI improves its truthfulness from 32.5% to 65.1%. We identify a tradeoff between truthfulness and helpfulness and demonstrate how to balance it by tuning the intervention strength. ITI is minimally invasive and computationally inexpensive. Moreover, the technique is data efficient: while approaches like RLHF require extensive annotations, ITI locates truthful directions using only few hundred examples. Our findings suggest that LLMs may have an internal representation of the likelihood of something being true, even as they produce falsehoods on the surface.

papers.title: Large Language Models as Model Organisms for Human Associative Learning
papers.research_question: Do LLMs exhibit representational dynamics akin to human associative learning, and can they help disambiguate between competing hypotheses for representational change? How does vocabulary interference modulate representational change?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs exhibit a non-monotonic pattern of representational change during associative learning (consistent with the Non-Monotonic Plasticity Hypothesis), and this change is modulated by vocabulary interference, with higher interference leading to stronger differentiation.
papers.conclusion: LLMs can serve as accessible and general computational models for studying human associative learning, providing new insights into how local pair similarity and global competition shape representational change.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs show three distinct phases of learning during in-context associative learning: encoding (accuracy increases), consolidation (accuracy stabilizes), and forgetting (accuracy declines).
During the consolidation phase, moderately similar token pairs significantly differentiate, producing a U-shaped pattern of representational change that aligns with the Non-Monotonic Plasticity Hypothesis.
Vocabulary interference—the similarity between a paired item and the model's prior knowledge—modulates representational change: higher interference leads to stronger differentiation.
The non-monotonic differentiation pattern is only present during consolidation and disappears during encoding and forgetting phases.
These representational dynamics are consistent across six different open-source LLMs, despite architectural differences.
papers.limitation:
The token pairs used are synthetic and optimized for similarity, which may not reflect naturalistic learning scenarios.
The forgetting phase is not well understood, and its causes require further investigation.
LLMs are not biologically plausible models of the brain, limiting direct comparisons to neural mechanisms.
future_direction: Investigating the causes of forgetting and predicting when it occurs.
Extending the analysis to more naturalistic stimuli and real-world associative learning tasks.
Exploring how different model architectures (e.g., with explicit memory modules) affect representational dynamics.
papers.abstract: Associative learning--forming links between co-occurring items--is fundamental to human cognition, reshaping internal representations in complex ways. Testing hypotheses on how representational changes occur in biological systems is challenging, but large language models (LLMs) offer a scalable alternative. Building on LLMs' in-context learning, we adapt a cognitive neuroscience associative learning paradigm and investigate how representations evolve across six models. Our initial findings reveal a non-monotonic pattern consistent with the Non-Monotonic Plasticity Hypothesis, with moderately similar items differentiating after learning. Leveraging the controllability of LLMs, we further show that this differentiation is modulated by the overlap of associated items with the broader vocabulary--a factor we term vocabulary interference, capturing how new associations compete with prior knowledge. We find that higher vocabulary interference amplifies differentiation, suggesting that representational change is influenced by both item similarity and global competition. Our findings position LLMs not only as powerful tools for studying representational dynamics in human-like learning systems, but also as accessible and general computational models for generating new hypotheses about the principles underlying memory reorganization in the brain.

papers.title: Rethinking Robustness: A New Approach to Evaluating Feature Attribution Methods
papers.research_question: How can we evaluate the robustness of feature attribution methods in a way that is independent of the model's adversarial robustness and training quality?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a new definition of similar inputs for evaluating attributional robustness, a new robustness metric (OSR) that decouples attributional robustness from adversarial robustness, and a GAN-based method to generate similar inputs.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that a more objective metric is needed to evaluate attribution methods independently of the neural network's robustness, and the proposed OSR metric is a step in that direction.
papers.key_findings:
Existing attributional robustness metrics are biased by the model's adversarial robustness and training quality, leading to inconsistent rankings of attribution methods.
The proposed OSR metric ranks attribution methods consistently across well-trained and poorly-trained models, unlike existing metrics.
The GAN-based method generates inputs that are similar in the model's output space, providing a more objective testbed for evaluating attribution methods.
There is a trade-off between robustness and fidelity for some attribution methods, with methods like SmoothGrad showing high robustness but low fidelity.
future_direction: Further development and use of the OSR metric.
Further efforts to disentangle attributional robustness from adversarial robustness.
Exploring the relationship between bounded inputs and bounded outputs concerning similarity for attributional robustness.
papers.abstract: This paper studies the robustness of feature attribution methods for deep neural networks. It challenges the current notion of attributional robustness that largely ignores the difference in the model's outputs and introduces a new way of evaluating the robustness of attribution methods. Specifically, we propose a new definition of similar inputs, a new robustness metric, and a novel method based on generative adversarial networks to generate these inputs. In addition, we present a comprehensive evaluation with existing metrics and state-of-the-art attribution methods. Our findings highlight the need for a more objective metric that reveals the weaknesses of an attribution method rather than that of the neural network, thus providing a more accurate evaluation of the robustness of attribution methods.

papers.title: Knowledge Accumulation in Continually Learned Representations and the Issue of Feature Forgetting
papers.research_question: Do continually trained representations forget catastrophically? What are the consequences of forgetting these representations?
papers.core_contribution: This paper shows that, when measured relative to performance gained during a task, forgetting in continually learned representations is as catastrophic as at the output level, except for information shared across tasks. It also demonstrates that this feature forgetting substantially hinders the accumulation of general knowledge.
papers.conclusion: Representations in continually trained neural networks forget catastrophically when considering relative forgetting, and this feature forgetting impedes the efficient accumulation of general knowledge. Preventing feature forgetting is crucial for learning strong representations over time.
papers.key_findings:
Continually learned representations exhibit two key phenomena: feature forgetting (loss of task-specific information) and knowledge accumulation (improvement on unseen tasks).
Relative forgetting (forgetting relative to performance gained during a task) reveals that representations forget newly learned information as catastrophically as the output layer, except for the first few tasks.
Information that is not forgotten from early tasks is information that is shared and can be re-learned from later tasks, as shown by task exclusion experiments.
Feature forgetting slows down knowledge accumulation, as demonstrated by an ensemble baseline that avoids forgetting and achieves much better general representations.
Among continual learning methods, functional regularization (e.g., MAS, LwF) is most effective at reducing feature forgetting and promoting knowledge accumulation.
papers.abstract: Continual learning research has shown that neural networks suffer from catastrophic forgetting "at the output level", but it is debated whether this is also the case at the level of learned representations. Multiple recent studies ascribe representations a certain level of innate robustness against forgetting -- that they only forget minimally in comparison with forgetting at the output level. We revisit and expand upon the experiments that revealed this difference in forgetting and illustrate the coexistence of two phenomena that affect the quality of continually learned representations: knowledge accumulation and feature forgetting. Taking both aspects into account, we show that, even though forgetting in the representation (i.e. feature forgetting) can be small in absolute terms, when measuring relative to how much was learned during a task, forgetting in the representation tends to be just as catastrophic as forgetting at the output level. Next we show that this feature forgetting is problematic as it substantially slows down the incremental learning of good general representations (i.e. knowledge accumulation). Finally, we study how feature forgetting and knowledge accumulation are affected by different types of continual learning methods.

papers.title: Hidden Breakthroughs in Language Model Training
papers.research_question: How can we identify hidden breakthroughs in language model training that are obscured by the aggregate loss curve?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces POLCA, a method to decompose loss changes along basis vectors to identify hidden breakthroughs and skill acquisition during model training.
papers.conclusion: POLCA clustering identifies learned skills from decomposed loss trajectories and supports the hypothesis that high-dimensional learning involves a series of breakthroughs at various scales.
papers.key_findings:
POLCA can identify hidden breakthroughs in training that are not visible in the aggregate loss curve.
In arithmetic addition, POLCA clustering recovers the carry skill, which is not recoverable from exact loss curves.
In language modeling, POLCA clustering reveals clusters corresponding to grammatical constructions like appositive noun phrases.
The method demonstrates that models undergo multiple breakthroughs at different scales during training.
POLCA provides a tool for unsupervised interpretability by identifying skill acquisition events.
papers.limitation: The trained models may contain biases from the training datasets.
papers.abstract: Loss curves are smooth during most of model training, so visible discontinuities stand out as possible conceptual breakthroughs. Studying these breakthroughs enables a deeper understanding of learning dynamics, but only when they are properly identified. This paper argues that similar breakthroughs occur frequently throughout training but they are obscured by a loss metric that collapses all variation into a single scalar. To find these hidden transitions, we introduce POLCA, a method for decomposing changes in loss along arbitrary bases of the low-rank training subspace. We use our method to identify clusters of samples that share similar changes in loss during training, disaggregating the overall loss into that of smaller groups of conceptually similar data. We validate our method on synthetic arithmetic and natural language tasks, showing that POLCA recovers clusters that represent interpretable breakthroughs in the model's capabilities. We demonstrate the promise of these hidden phase transitions as a tool for unsupervised interpretability.

papers.title: Emergent Introspective Awareness in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Does this paper investigate whether large language models can introspect on their internal states.
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that large language models possess some functional introspective awareness of their internal states through concept injection experiments.
papers.conclusion: Current language models have limited but functional introspective awareness, which is unreliable but may improve with model capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
Models can detect and identify injected concepts in their activations.
Models can distinguish between injected thoughts and text inputs.
Models can use introspection to detect artificially prefilled outputs.
Models can modulate their internal representations when instructed to think about concepts.
Introspective capabilities are more pronounced in more capable models like Claude Opus 4 and 4.1.
papers.limitation:
The abilities observed are highly unreliable; failures of introspection remain the norm.
Experiments do not pin down specific mechanistic explanations.
Concept injection places models in an unnatural setting.
future_direction: Identifying metacognitive representations more clearly
Investigating the grounding of emotional responses in introspective reports
Exploring introspective capabilities in more natural conditions
papers.abstract: We investigate whether large language models can introspect on their internal states. It is difficult to answer this question through conversation alone, as genuine introspection cannot be distinguished from confabulations. Here, we address this challenge by injecting representations of known concepts into a model's activations, and measuring the influence of these manipulations on the model's self-reported states. We find that models can, in certain scenarios, notice the presence of injected concepts and accurately identify them. Models demonstrate some ability to recall prior internal representations and distinguish them from raw text inputs. Strikingly, we find that some models can use their ability to recall prior intentions in order to distinguish their own outputs from artificial prefills. In all these experiments, Claude Opus 4 and 4.1, the most capable models we tested, generally demonstrate the greatest introspective awareness; however, trends across models are complex and sensitive to post-training strategies. Finally, we explore whether models can explicitly control their internal representations, finding that models can modulate their activations when instructed or incentivized to "think about" a concept. Overall, our results indicate that current language models possess some functional introspective awareness of their own internal states. We stress that in today's models, this capacity is highly unreliable and context-dependent; however, it may continue to develop with further improvements to model capabilities.

papers.title: Scaling Competence, Shrinking Reasoning: Cognitive Signatures in Language Model Learning
papers.research_question: How do reasoning tokens evolve during fine-tuning, and can they serve as indicators of learning stages?
papers.core_contribution: Reasoning tokens in language models expand, peak, and contract during fine-tuning, mirroring the Four Stages of Competence, and their dynamics can serve as metrics for diagnosing training stages and guiding early stopping.
papers.conclusion: Reasoning tokens serve as a dynamic scaffold during fine-tuning, providing insights into model learning dynamics and practical tools for diagnosing training progress and optimizing learning strategies.
papers.key_findings:
Reasoning token length increases with performance early in training, peaks at conscious competence, then declines as the model internalizes the task.
Models retain task performance after training even when reasoning tokens are removed, indicating that reasoning scaffolds learning but becomes unnecessary once competence is acquired.
The progression of reasoning tokens aligns with the Four Stages of Competence framework from cognitive science.
Reasoning token dynamics can diagnose training stages, detect convergence, and inform early stopping criteria.
The pattern is consistent across multiple models and tasks including code generation, math problems, and logical question answering.
papers.limitation:
Reasoning token length and correctness are surface-level proxies for internal cognitive processes, and the use of competence stages is interpretive rather than diagnostic.
Experiments are limited to math, logic, and code generation tasks, and may not generalize to tasks with high ambiguity or contextual sensitivity.
The proposed metrics may be less stable in settings with noisy supervision, curriculum learning, or large-scale instruction tuning.
future_direction: Future work may formalize these analogies further or challenge them with deeper mechanistic analysis.
papers.abstract: We analyze reasoning in language models during task-specific fine-tuning and draws parallel between reasoning tokens--intermediate steps generated while solving problem and the human working memory. Drawing from cognitive science, we align training dynamics with the Four Stages of Competence: models initially produce incorrect outputs without reasoning, then begin reasoning (but still fail), eventually reason effectively, and finally solve tasks without explicit reasoning. We find that reasoning token length expands as performance improves, peaks at the stage of conscious competence, then declines as the model internalizes the task. Notably, after training, models retain performance even when reasoning is removed--suggesting it scaffolded learning but is no longer needed. This progression offers actionable insights: reasoning token dynamics can serve as a signal for diagnosing training stage, identifying convergence, and guiding early stopping. We propose metrics to track this trajectory and argue that reasoning behavior is valuable for understanding and optimizing reasoning model training.

papers.title: Unforgettable Generalization in Language Models
papers.research_question: What happens when language models are trained to forget a skill via fine-tuning on randomized labels? How does forgetting generalize to examples outside the training set?
papers.core_contribution: Random-label forgetting does not generalize equally across tasks; forgetting is task-dependent and shallow, as linear probes can still recover task information from hidden states after forgetting.
papers.conclusion: Random-label forgetting is an unpredictable and shallow method for skill removal, highlighting the difficulty of targeted unlearning in language models.
papers.key_findings:
Forgetting generalization varies across tasks: entailment classification tasks are more forgettable, while commonsense reasoning tasks are more resilient.
The effectiveness of forgetting is largely determined by the evaluation task, not the training task used for forgetting.
Dataset difficulty is not predictive of whether a task can be forgotten.
Model confidence and the variance of hidden state representations are weakly predictive of the degree of forgetting.
Forgetting is shallow: linear probes trained on hidden states can still perform the task reliably after forgetting, indicating information is not removed from representations.
future_direction: Understanding which specific examples are forgotten and why
Further research on the relationship between training data and forgetting
papers.abstract: When language models (LMs) are trained to forget (or "unlearn'') a skill, how precisely does their behavior change? We study the behavior of transformer LMs in which tasks have been forgotten via fine-tuning on randomized labels. Such LMs learn to generate near-random predictions for individual examples in the "training'' set used for forgetting. Across tasks, however, LMs exhibit extreme variability in whether LM predictions change on examples outside the training set. In some tasks (like entailment classification), forgetting generalizes robustly, and causes models to produce uninformative predictions on new task instances; in other tasks (like physical commonsense reasoning and scientific question answering) forgetting affects only the training examples, and models continue to perform the "forgotten'' task accurately even for examples very similar to those that appeared in the training set. Dataset difficulty is not predictive of whether a behavior can be forgotten; instead, generalization in forgetting is (weakly) predicted by the confidence of LMs' initial task predictions and the variability of LM representations of training data, with low confidence and low variability both associated with greater generalization. Perhaps most surprisingly, random-label forgetting appears to be somewhat insensitive to the contents of the training set: for example, models trained on science questions with random labels continue to answer other science questions accurately, but begin to produce random labels on entailment classification tasks. Finally, we show that even generalizable forgetting is shallow: linear probes trained on LMs' representations can still perform tasks reliably after forgetting. Our results highlight the difficulty and unpredictability of performing targeted skill removal from models via fine-tuning.

papers.title: Distilled Circuits: A Mechanistic Study of Internal Restructuring in Knowledge Distillation
papers.research_question: How does knowledge distillation restructure internal circuits and representations in student models, and how can functional alignment between teacher and student be quantified?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides a mechanistic understanding of how knowledge distillation restructures internal circuits, showing that students compress and discard teacher components, and introduces an alignment metric to quantify functional alignment beyond output similarity.
papers.conclusion: While student models preserve broad functional behavior from their teachers, knowledge distillation causes significant internal circuit restructuring, leading to increased reliance on fewer components and reduced robustness. The alignment metric captures functional similarity beyond output behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Student models reorganize, compress, and discard teacher components, leading to stronger reliance on fewer components.
Student models are more vulnerable to component ablation, indicating reduced robustness.
The introduced alignment metric effectively quantifies functional alignment between teacher and student models.
These findings on internal restructuring and reduced robustness generalize across different model architectures (GPT2, BERT, Llama).
Performance similarity does not guarantee similarity in internal computation; circuit-level analysis is essential for understanding functional alignment.
papers.limitation:
The study is constrained by the relatively small set of models evaluated (6).
The component role attribution procedure is manual and could be automated.
The alignment metric could be improved in granularity and interpretability.
The findings are based on specific tasks and models and may not generalize to all settings.
future_direction: Apply the methodology and alignment metric to a broader, more diverse collection of models.
Automate the component role attribution procedure, potentially using interpretability agents.
Improve the alignment metric's granularity and interpretability, and explore incorporating it as a loss term during distillation.
papers.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses a larger neural model (teacher) into smaller, faster student models by training them to match teacher outputs. However, the internal computational transformations that occur during this process remain poorly understood. We apply techniques from mechanistic interpretability to analyze how internal circuits, representations, and activation patterns differ between teacher and student. Focusing on GPT2-small and its distilled counterpart DistilGPT2, we find that student models reorganize, compress, and discard teacher components, often resulting in stronger reliance on fewer individual components. To quantify functional alignment beyond output similarity, we introduce an alignment metric based on influence-weighted component similarity, validated across multiple tasks. Our findings reveal that while knowledge distillation preserves broad functional behaviors, it also causes significant shifts in internal computation, with important implications for the robustness and generalization capacity of distilled models.

papers.title: Dynamic Neural Turing Machine with Soft and Hard Addressing Schemes
papers.research_question: How can neural Turing machines be extended with a trainable memory addressing scheme to learn a wide variety of location-based addressing strategies, and how do continuous versus discrete addressing mechanisms affect performance on tasks like episodic question-answering?
papers.core_contribution: The paper extends the Neural Turing Machine (NTM) into a Dynamic Neural Turing Machine (D-NTM) by introducing a trainable memory addressing scheme with separate address and content vectors, enabling learning of nonlinear location-based addressing. It also shows that discrete addressing can outperform continuous addressing on tasks requiring precise memory retrieval.
papers.conclusion: The Dynamic Neural Turing Machine (D-NTM) with a learnable addressing scheme and discrete attention mechanism is an effective extension of NTM, demonstrating improved performance on a range of tasks including episodic QA, sequential classification, natural language inference, and algorithmic problems.
papers.key_findings:
D-NTM with a learnable addressing scheme outperforms the original NTM and LSTM baselines on the Facebook bAbI episodic question-answering tasks.
Discrete (non-differentiable) addressing with a GRU controller often works better than continuous (differentiable) addressing, especially for tasks requiring precise retrieval of stored facts.
A curriculum learning strategy that anneals from continuous to discrete attention helps train feedforward controllers with discrete attention, significantly reducing error rates.
D-NTM performs well on sequential pMNIST, SNLI, and algorithmic tasks (copy and associative recall), demonstrating its ability to handle long-term dependencies and various problem types.
The model's performance is still weaker than memory networks that store facts explicitly without modification, highlighting the difficulty of learning to write and manipulate memory content.
papers.limitation: NTM-based models, including D-NTM, are weaker than memory networks that store incoming facts explicitly without modification, due to the difficulty of learning how to write, manipulate, and delete memory content.
future_direction: Apply the learnable address and discrete addressing schemes to a wider array of memory-based models beyond neural Turing machines.
Evaluate the proposed D-NTM on a diverse set of applications such as text summarization, visual question-answering, and machine translation.
papers.abstract: We extend neural Turing machine (NTM) model into a dynamic neural Turing machine (D-NTM) by introducing a trainable memory addressing scheme. This addressing scheme maintains for each memory cell two separate vectors, content and address vectors. This allows the D-NTM to learn a wide variety of location-based addressing strategies including both linear and nonlinear ones. We implement the D-NTM with both continuous, differentiable and discrete, non-differentiable read/write mechanisms. We investigate the mechanisms and effects of learning to read and write into a memory through experiments on Facebook bAbI tasks using both a feedforward and GRUcontroller. The D-NTM is evaluated on a set of Facebook bAbI tasks and shown to outperform NTM and LSTM baselines. We have done extensive analysis of our model and different variations of NTM on bAbI task. We also provide further experimental results on sequential pMNIST, Stanford Natural Language Inference, associative recall and copy tasks.

papers.title: Sudden Drops in the Loss: Syntax Acquisition, Phase Transitions, and Simplicity Bias in MLMs
papers.research_question: How does syntactic attention structure (SAS) emerge during training of masked language models, and what is its causal role in the development of grammatical capabilities?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that syntactic attention structure (SAS) emerges abruptly during training and is necessary for grammatical capabilities; briefly suppressing SAS early in training can improve model quality by allowing an alternative strategy to emerge.
papers.conclusion: Developmental analysis of training dynamics is crucial for understanding model behavior, and SAS represents a simplicity bias that can be manipulated to improve training.
papers.key_findings:
SAS emerges abruptly during training in a phase transition called the structure onset.
The structure onset precedes and is necessary for the capabilities onset, which marks improvements in grammatical capabilities.
Suppressing SAS throughout training prevents the development of grammatical capabilities.
Briefly suppressing SAS early in training improves model quality and accelerates convergence.
There exists an alternative strategy that competes with SAS, and suppressing SAS allows this alternative strategy to emerge earlier.
papers.abstract: Most interpretability research in NLP focuses on understanding the behavior and features of a fully trained model. However, certain insights into model behavior may only be accessible by observing the trajectory of the training process. We present a case study of syntax acquisition in masked language models (MLMs) that demonstrates how analyzing the evolution of interpretable artifacts throughout training deepens our understanding of emergent behavior. In particular, we study Syntactic Attention Structure (SAS), a naturally emerging property of MLMs wherein specific Transformer heads tend to focus on specific syntactic relations. We identify a brief window in pretraining when models abruptly acquire SAS, concurrent with a steep drop in loss. This breakthrough precipitates the subsequent acquisition of linguistic capabilities. We then examine the causal role of SAS by manipulating SAS during training, and demonstrate that SAS is necessary for the development of grammatical capabilities. We further find that SAS competes with other beneficial traits during training, and that briefly suppressing SAS improves model quality. These findings offer an interpretation of a real-world example of both simplicity bias and breakthrough training dynamics.

papers.title: Study of Pretraining Bias and Frequencies
papers.research_question: How do pretraining term frequencies and pretraining bias impact the performance of language models in an in-context learning setting?
papers.core_contribution: The performance of language models in in-context learning is significantly influenced by the pretraining frequencies of terms in demonstrations, and models can overcome pretraining bias when provided with more demonstrations.
papers.conclusion: Pretraining data has a significant impact on in-context learning performance, and language models can overcome pretraining bias when provided with more demonstrations that illustrate the correct input-output mapping.
papers.key_findings:
Model performance on arithmetic tasks is positively correlated with the pretraining frequency of the numbers involved.
Using high-frequency numbers in few-shot demonstrations can improve task performance.
With random demonstrations, model performance initially relies on pretraining bias but decreases with more shots as the model starts to learn the input-output mapping.
In adversarial demonstrations (e.g., prompting for subtraction when biased towards addition), the model can overcome its pretraining bias as the number of shots increases.
Reinforcement learning finetuning provides only minor improvements, with primary learning stemming from pretraining and supervised finetuning.
future_direction: Improving the learning capabilities of language models in low-frequency environments.
Studying the difference between embeddings of high-frequency and low-frequency numbers.
Building hybrid applications that use language models for high-frequency computations and external APIs for low-frequency environments.
papers.abstract: Usage of language models in an in-context learning environment has been adapted for a wide range of tasks. Recent works have showcased the impact of pretraining data on the in-context performance of language models. In this work, we experiment with numbers having high and low frequencies in the pretraining data to understand the impact of term frequencies on the model's performance. We also experiment with random and adversarial demonstrations to understand the pretraining bias present in the model. Through these experiments, we showcase the importance of pretraining frequencies of the numbers present in the demonstrations and explain how highly frequent terms can be used in the demonstrations to achieve better task performance. Moreover, we also show the impact of pretraining bias on the model's performance and explain how the model overcomes this bias with more demonstrations.

papers.title: Influence Dynamics and Stagewise Data Attribution
papers.research_question: How does the influence of training data on model behavior change dynamically over the course of training, challenging the static view of influence functions?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a framework for stagewise data attribution based on singular learning theory, showing that influence of training data changes dynamically during learning, with non-monotonic changes and peaks at developmental phase transitions.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that influence is dynamic and stagewise, challenging the static view of influence functions, and proposes stagewise data attribution as a new framework for understanding data impact during learning.
papers.key_findings:
Influence is not static but changes non-monotonically over training, including sign flips and sharp peaks at developmental transitions.
In a toy model of hierarchical feature learning, dynamic shifts in influence correspond to the model's progressive learning of semantic hierarchy.
In language models, token-level influence changes align with known developmental stages, such as the formation of induction circuits.
The Bayesian Influence Function (BIF) is a suitable tool for measuring influence in singular models, as it is Hessian-free and well-defined throughout training.
Stagewise data attribution provides a new perspective on when and why data matters during learning, moving beyond static attribution.
papers.limitation: The Bayesian Influence Function requires careful hyperparameter tuning for accurate estimation, as shown in the hyperparameter sweep.
papers.abstract: Current training data attribution (TDA) methods treat the influence one sample has on another as static, but neural networks learn in distinct stages that exhibit changing patterns of influence. In this work, we introduce a framework for stagewise data attribution grounded in singular learning theory. We predict that influence can change non-monotonically, including sign flips and sharp peaks at developmental transitions. We first validate these predictions analytically and empirically in a toy model, showing that dynamic shifts in influence directly map to the model's progressive learning of a semantic hierarchy. Finally, we demonstrate these phenomena at scale in language models, where token-level influence changes align with known developmental stages.

papers.title: Language Models Are Capable of Metacognitive Monitoring and Control of Their Internal Activations
papers.research_question: Can LLMs accurately monitor and control their internal neural activations? Why can they report some intermediate steps but not others?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a neurofeedback paradigm to quantify metacognitive abilities in LLMs, showing they can report and control internal activations along certain axes, with performance depending on interpretability, variance, and context.
papers.conclusion: LLMs have limited metacognitive abilities to monitor and control their internal activations, which raises important considerations for AI safety and alignment.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs can report neural activations along target axes, with performance improving with more in-context examples and being better for semantically interpretable axes.
LLMs can explicitly and implicitly control neural activations, with explicit control being stronger and effects increasing with model size and depth.
Control effects are stronger for axes with semantic interpretability and those explaining more variance.
The axes that can be reported and controlled span a low-dimensional 'metacognitive space'.
Metacognitive abilities have implications for AI safety, as models might evade neural-based oversight.
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to instruction-fine-tuned models and may not generalize to base models.
The neurofeedback paradigm assumes the model can understand the task, which may not hold for all models or tasks.
future_direction: Extend the neurofeedback paradigm to more models and datasets.
Investigate the neural mechanisms underlying metacognitive control in LLMs.
Explore applications in AI safety, such as developing better oversight methods.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can sometimes report the strategies they actually use to solve tasks, yet at other times seem unable to recognize those strategies that govern their behavior. This suggests a limited degree of metacognition - the capacity to monitor one's own cognitive processes for subsequent reporting and self-control. Metacognition enhances LLMs' capabilities in solving complex tasks but also raises safety concerns, as models may obfuscate their internal processes to evade neural-activation-based oversight (e.g., safety detector). Given society's increased reliance on these models, it is critical that we understand their metacognitive abilities. To address this, we introduce a neuroscience-inspired neurofeedback paradigm that uses in-context learning to quantify metacognitive abilities of LLMs to report and control their activation patterns. We demonstrate that their abilities depend on several factors: the number of in-context examples provided, the semantic interpretability of the neural activation direction (to be reported/controlled), and the variance explained by that direction.
