papers.abstract: We analyze the storage and recall of factual associations in autoregressive transformer language models, finding evidence that these associations correspond to localized, directly-editable computations. We first develop a causal intervention for identifying neuron activations that are decisive in a model's factual predictions. This reveals a distinct set of steps in middle-layer feed-forward modules that mediate factual predictions while processing subject tokens. To test our hypothesis that these computations correspond to factual association recall, we modify feed-forward weights to update specific factual associations using Rank-One Model Editing (ROME). We find that ROME is effective on a standard zero-shot relation extraction (zsRE) model-editing task, comparable to existing methods. To perform a more sensitive evaluation, we also evaluate ROME on a new dataset of counterfactual assertions, on which it simultaneously maintains both specificity and generalization, whereas other methods sacrifice one or another. Our results confirm an important role for mid-layer feed-forward modules in storing factual associations and suggest that direct manipulation of computational mechanisms may be a feasible approach for model editing. The code, dataset, visualizations, and an interactive demo notebook are available at https://rome.baulab.info/

papers.title: LMEnt: A Suite for Analyzing Knowledge in Language Models from Pretraining Data to Representations
papers.research_question: How do language models acquire and represent knowledge from pretraining data, and what is the interplay between data composition, training dynamics, and internal knowledge mechanisms?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces LMEnt, a suite for analyzing knowledge acquisition in language models, including annotated pretraining data, entity-based retrieval, and pretrained models, enabling studies on the connection between data and knowledge representations.
papers.conclusion: LMEnt provides a flexible testbed for investigating knowledge representations in language models and facilitates future research on knowledge acquisition and editing.
papers.key_findings:
LMEnt's entity-based retrieval outperforms string-based methods by up to 80.4% in returning relevant document chunks.
LMEnt models achieve comparable knowledge recall performance to models trained on orders of magnitude more data.
Knowledge acquisition is correlated with fact frequency, but both learning and forgetting rates increase with frequency.
Increasing model size improves learning of frequent facts but has little effect on tail facts.
papers.limitation:
Pretraining data is relatively small and models are compute-efficient, which may limit generalizability.
Does not compare with dense retrievers like DPR or ColBERT.
Focuses only on pretraining, not mid- or post-training phases.
future_direction: Investigating knowledge plasticity and editing during pretraining.
Improving factuality of LMs using entity annotations.
Extending LMEnt to other data sources and architectures.
papers.abstract: Language models (LMs) increasingly drive real-world applications that require world knowledge. However, the internal processes through which models turn data into representations of knowledge and beliefs about the world, are poorly understood. Insights into these processes could pave the way for developing LMs with knowledge representations that are more consistent, robust, and complete. To facilitate studying these questions, we present LMEnt, a suite for analyzing knowledge acquisition in LMs during pretraining. LMEnt introduces: (1) a knowledge-rich pretraining corpus, fully annotated with entity mentions, based on Wikipedia, (2) an entity-based retrieval method over pretraining data that outperforms previous approaches by as much as 80.4%, and (3) 12 pretrained models with up to 1B parameters and 4K intermediate checkpoints, with comparable performance to popular open-sourced models on knowledge benchmarks. Together, these resources provide a controlled environment for analyzing connections between entity mentions in pretraining and downstream performance, and the effects of causal interventions in pretraining data. We show the utility of LMEnt by studying knowledge acquisition across checkpoints, finding that fact frequency is key, but does not fully explain learning trends. We release LMEnt to support studies of knowledge in LMs, including knowledge representations, plasticity, editing, attribution, and learning dynamics.

papers.title: A Note on Normalized Emergence Timing (in Pythia Language Model Evaluations)
papers.research_question: How do large language models (LLMs) develop and evolve over the course of training? How do these patterns change as models scale?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Pythia, a suite of 16 LLMs trained on public data in the same order with 154 checkpoints each, and provides tools to reconstruct exact training dataloaders, enabling controlled studies on training dynamics and scaling.
papers.conclusion: The highly controlled setup of the Pythia suite can yield novel insights into LLMs and their training dynamics, facilitating future research.
papers.key_findings:
Gender bias can be reduced by swapping pronouns in the last portion of training, with larger models showing greater reduction.
Memorization follows a Poisson point process and is not influenced by the location of a sequence in the training data.
The impact of pretraining term frequencies on few-shot performance emerges after a phase change at 65,000 steps for models with 2.8B parameters or more.
papers.limitation: The noisiness in the progression of gender bias metrics may reflect actual changes or poor reliability of the CrowS-Pairs benchmark.
future_direction: Further study of interventions (modifying training data) for bias mitigation and other applications.
Investigation of the reliability of the CrowS-Pairs benchmark.
papers.abstract: How do large language models (LLMs) develop and evolve over the course of training? How do these patterns change as models scale? To answer these questions, we introduce \textit{Pythia}, a suite of 16 LLMs all trained on public data seen in the exact same order and ranging in size from 70M to 12B parameters. We provide public access to 154 checkpoints for each one of the 16 models, alongside tools to download and reconstruct their exact training dataloaders for further study. We intend \textit{Pythia} to facilitate research in many areas, and we present several case studies including novel results in memorization, term frequency effects on few-shot performance, and reducing gender bias. We demonstrate that this highly controlled setup can be used to yield novel insights toward LLMs and their training dynamics. Trained models, analysis code, training code, and training data can be found at \url{https://github.com/EleutherAI/pythia}.

papers.title: Crosscoding Through Time: Tracking Emergence & Consolidation Of Linguistic Representations Throughout LLM Pretraining
papers.research_question: How do linguistic features emerge and evolve during the pretraining of large language models?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces a method using sparse crosscoders and the Relative Indirect Effect (RELIE) metric to track the emergence and evolution of linguistic features during LLM pretraining.
papers.conclusion: The approach is architecture-agnostic and scalable, offering a promising path toward more interpretable and fine-grained analysis of representation learning throughout pretraining.
papers.key_findings:
Crosscoders can detect feature emergence, maintenance, and discontinuation during pretraining.
Features evolve from token-specific detectors to abstract syntactic concepts over training time.
The Relative Indirect Effect (RELIE) metric effectively traces the causal importance of features across checkpoints.
The method is architecture-agnostic and scalable to billion-parameter models.
Multilingual models develop cross-lingual feature sharing, with abstract concepts becoming more universal over time.
papers.limitation: Early checkpoints may resist sparse mapping and accurate reconstruction with crosscoders.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) learn non-trivial abstractions during pretraining, like detecting irregular plural noun subjects. However, it is not well understood when and how specific linguistic abilities emerge as traditional evaluation methods such as benchmarking fail to reveal how models acquire concepts and capabilities. To bridge this gap and better understand model training at the concept level, we use sparse crosscoders to discover and align features across model checkpoints. Using this approach, we track the evolution of linguistic features during pretraining. We train crosscoders between open-sourced checkpoint triplets with significant performance and representation shifts, and introduce a novel metric, Relative Indirect Effects (RelIE), to trace training stages at which individual features become causally important for task performance. We show that crosscoders can detect feature emergence, maintenance, and discontinuation during pretraining. Our approach is architecture-agnostic and scalable, offering a promising path toward more interpretable and fine-grained analysis of representation learning throughout pretraining.

papers.title: Understanding the Behaviors of BERT in Ranking
papers.research_question: What are the performances and behaviors of BERT in ranking tasks on MS MARCO and TREC Web Track?
papers.core_contribution: BERT is effective for QA-focused passage ranking due to its interaction-based seq2seq matching, but less effective for ad hoc document ranking where user click signals are more beneficial.
papers.conclusion: BERT excels in seq2seq matching tasks like MS MARCO due to its pre-training on surrounding contexts, but for ad hoc document ranking, pre-training on user clicks is more effective.
papers.key_findings:
BERT-based rankers outperform previous neural IR models on MS MARCO passage ranking.
BERT is not effective as a representation-based model for ranking; it relies on cross-sequence interactions.
On TREC ad hoc ranking, BERT underperforms compared to feature-based learning to rank and models pre-trained on user clicks.
BERT's attention focuses on marker tokens and stopwords, but stopwords have minimal impact on performance.
BERT assigns extreme ranking scores and depends on a few key terms, preferring semantic matches over loose relevance.
papers.limitation: BERT performs worse on TREC ad hoc ranking compared to models pre-trained on user clicks, indicating a gap between its pre-training on surrounding contexts and the needs of document ranking.
future_direction: Training deeper networks on user clicks signals
Studying deeper models trained on relevance-based labels compared to shallower neural rankers
papers.abstract: This paper studies the performances and behaviors of BERT in ranking tasks. We explore several different ways to leverage the pre-trained BERT and fine-tune it on two ranking tasks: MS MARCO passage reranking and TREC Web Track ad hoc document ranking. Experimental results on MS MARCO demonstrate the strong effectiveness of BERT in question-answering focused passage ranking tasks, as well as the fact that BERT is a strong interaction-based seq2seq matching model. Experimental results on TREC show the gaps between the BERT pre-trained on surrounding contexts and the needs of ad hoc document ranking. Analyses illustrate how BERT allocates its attentions between query-document tokens in its Transformer layers, how it prefers semantic matches between paraphrase tokens, and how that differs with the soft match patterns learned by a click-trained neural ranker.

papers.title: Biologically Plausible, Human‐Scale Knowledge Representation
papers.research_question: Can a neurally plausible model represent and manipulate structured knowledge at a human scale, specifically by encoding and decoding the main lexical relations in WordNet?
papers.core_contribution: The paper presents a biologically plausible spiking neural network that uses a Vector Symbolic Architecture (VSA) to successfully encode and decode the structured knowledge in WordNet, demonstrating human-scale knowledge representation with plausible neural resource requirements.
papers.conclusion: The results demonstrate that the presented approach is uniquely well-suited to providing a biologically plausible, human-scale account of the structured representations that underwrite cognition.
papers.key_findings:
The model achieved 100% accuracy in decoding individual WordNet concepts.
The model achieved 95.5% accuracy in traversing the WordNet hierarchy to arbitrary depth.
The model achieved 99.6% accuracy in decoding sentences constructed from WordNet concepts bound to roles.
The model uses about 2.5 million neurons, equivalent to approximately 14.7 mm² of cortex, which is biologically plausible and a significant improvement over prior approaches.
papers.abstract: Several approaches to implementing symbol-like representations in neurally plausible models have been proposed. These approaches include binding through synchrony (Shastri & Ajjanagadde, ), "mesh" binding (van der Velde & de Kamps, ), and conjunctive binding (Smolensky, ). Recent theoretical work has suggested that most of these methods will not scale well, that is, that they cannot encode structured representations using any of the tens of thousands of terms in the adult lexicon without making implausible resource assumptions. Here, we empirically demonstrate that the biologically plausible structured representations employed in the Semantic Pointer Architecture (SPA) approach to modeling cognition (Eliasmith, ) do scale appropriately. Specifically, we construct a spiking neural network of about 2.5 million neurons that employs semantic pointers to successfully encode and decode the main lexical relations in WordNet, which has over 100,000 terms. In addition, we show that the same representations can be employed to construct recursively structured sentences consisting of arbitrary WordNet concepts, while preserving the original lexical structure. We argue that these results suggest that semantic pointers are uniquely well-suited to providing a biologically plausible account of the structured representations that underwrite human cognition.

papers.title: Learning and Unlearning of Fabricated Knowledge in Language Models
papers.research_question: What happens when a new piece of knowledge is introduced into the training data and how long does it last while a large language model (LM) continues to train?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that knowledge-conflicting facts are most enduring in language models and proposes a sparsification method to erase them while preserving task performance.
papers.conclusion: The paper discovers that knowledge-conflicting facts endure for many updates and cause inappropriate priming, and shows that their impact can be mitigated via multi-step sparse updates while preserving main task training.
papers.key_findings:
Facts that conflict with common knowledge are remembered for tens of thousands of training steps, while mundane and scrambled facts are forgotten more rapidly.
Knowledge-conflicting facts can prime how the model hallucinates on logically unrelated prompts.
There is a sweet spot in fact novelty (between consistency and randomness) for memory durability.
The impact of knowledge-conflicting facts can be erased by multi-step sparse updates while preserving task performance.
future_direction: Extend the Outlandish dataset further
papers.abstract: What happens when a new piece of knowledge is introduced into the training data and how long does it last while a large language model (LM) continues to train? We investigate this question by injecting facts into LMs from a new probing dataset, "Outlandish", which is designed to permit the testing of a spectrum of different fact types. When studying how robust these memories are, there appears to be a sweet spot in the spectrum of fact novelty between consistency with world knowledge and total randomness, where the injected memory is the most enduring. Specifically we show that facts that conflict with common knowledge are remembered for tens of thousands of training steps, while prompts not conflicting with common knowledge (mundane), as well as scrambled prompts (randomly jumbled) are both forgotten much more rapidly. Further, knowledge-conflicting facts can "prime'' how the language model hallucinates on logically unrelated prompts, showing their propensity for non-target generalization, while both mundane and randomly jumbled facts prime significantly less. Finally, we show that impacts of knowledge-conflicting facts in LMs, though they can be long lasting, can be largely erased by novel application of multi-step sparse updates, even while the training ability of the model is preserved. As such, this very simple procedure has direct implications for mitigating the effects of data poisoning in training.

papers.title: Interpreting Pretrained Contextualized Representations via Reductions to Static Embeddings
papers.research_question: Can we convert pretrained contextualized representations to static embeddings to leverage mature static embedding interpretability methods, and what do we learn about representational quality and social bias through this process?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces simple, general methods for converting contextualized representations to static embeddings, enabling the use of static embedding interpretability methods. Analysis reveals that pooling over many contexts improves representational quality and that social bias is encoded disparately across models and layers.
papers.conclusion: Converting contextualized representations to static embeddings is a viable approach for interpretability, revealing important insights about representational quality and bias, and enabling the use of mature static embedding analysis methods.
papers.key_findings:
Pooling over many contexts (aggregated strategy) significantly improves the representational quality of static embeddings derived from contextualized models.
The best-performing layer for static embeddings shifts to later layers as the number of contexts increases.
Static embeddings derived from contextualized models can outperform traditional static embeddings like Word2Vec and GloVe on word similarity tasks.
Social bias is encoded disparately across different pretrained models and across different layers of the same model.
Existing bias estimators for word embeddings are dramatically inconsistent with each other.
papers.limitation:
The study only addresses a restricted subset of social biases and does not cover intersectional biases.
Existing bias estimators are inconsistent and may not reliably estimate bias.
future_direction: Investigate how the reduction to static embeddings affects different models and what it reflects about linguistic knowledge.
papers.abstract: Contextualized representations (e.g. ELMo, BERT) have become the default pretrained representations for downstream NLP applications. In some settings, this transition has rendered their static embedding predecessors (e.g. Word2Vec, GloVe) obsolete. As a side-effect, we observe that older interpretability methods for static embeddings -while more mature than those available for their dynamic counterparts -are underutilized in studying newer contextualized representations. Consequently, we introduce simple and fully general methods for converting from contextualized representations to static lookup-table embeddings which we apply to 5 popular pretrained models and 9 sets of pretrained weights. Our analysis of the resulting static embeddings notably reveals that pooling over many contexts significantly improves representational quality under intrinsic evaluation. Complementary to analyzing representational quality, we consider social biases encoded in pretrained representations with respect to gender, race/ethnicity, and religion and find that bias is encoded disparately across pretrained models and internal layers even for models that share the same training data. Concerningly, we find dramatic inconsistencies between social bias estimators for word embeddings.

papers.title: Memorization Without Overfitting: Analyzing the Training Dynamics of Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do memorization and forgetting dynamics in language models change during training, and how do they depend on factors like model size, dataset size, and learning rate?
papers.core_contribution: Larger language models memorize training data faster and forget less throughout training, with nouns and numbers being memorized more quickly than other parts of speech.
papers.conclusion: Memorization dynamics are a critical metric for understanding language model training, with larger models exhibiting faster memorization and less forgetting, highlighting the importance of analyzing memorization alongside cross-entropy loss.
papers.key_findings:
Larger language models memorize training data faster across various settings (causal and masked LM, different dataset sizes).
Larger models can memorize a larger portion of the data before overfitting occurs.
Forgetting curves approach a baseline (the forgetting baseline), and this baseline increases with model scale, meaning larger models forget less.
Nouns and numbers are memorized much faster than other parts of speech, acting as unique identifiers for training examples.
Adding unique identifiers (like document IDs) to training examples increases memorization speed.
papers.limitation:
The exact memorization metric (Definition 1) ignores model confidence and does not normalize for duplication in the training set.
The focus on exact memorization may not capture all aspects of privacy, as it only considers verbatim output of sensitive information.
future_direction: Understanding the structure of the forgetting baseline, e.g., what types of tokens (parts of speech, synonyms, facts) are memorized in the baseline.
Analyzing memorization dynamics as a critical metric when scaling up language models, beyond just cross-entropy loss.
papers.abstract: Despite their wide adoption, the underlying training and memorization dynamics of very large language models is not well understood. We empirically study exact memorization in causal and masked language modeling, across model sizes and throughout the training process. We measure the effects of dataset size, learning rate, and model size on memorization, finding that larger language models memorize training data faster across all settings. Surprisingly, we show that larger models can memorize a larger portion of the data before over-fitting and tend to forget less throughout the training process. We also analyze the memorization dynamics of different parts of speech and find that models memorize nouns and numbers first; we hypothesize and provide empirical evidence that nouns and numbers act as a unique identifier for memorizing individual training examples. Together, these findings present another piece of the broader puzzle of trying to understand what actually improves as models get bigger.

papers.title: Emergence of Hidden Capabilities: Exploring Learning Dynamics in Concept Space
papers.research_question: What determines the concepts a model learns, the order in which it learns them, and its ability to manipulate those concepts?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the concept space framework to analyze learning dynamics, showing that concept signal controls learning speed and order, and that hidden capabilities emerge suddenly during training before they can be elicited by naive prompting.
papers.conclusion: Generative models possess hidden capabilities that are learned suddenly and consistently during training, but naive input prompting may not elicit these capabilities, hence hiding how competent the model actually is.
papers.key_findings:
Concept signal (sensitivity of data-generating process to a concept) determines the speed at which a concept is learned.
Learning dynamics in concept space show sudden turns that correspond to the emergence of hidden capabilities.
Hidden capabilities (ability to generate out-of-distribution concept classes) can be elicited via latent interventions before they are accessible via naive prompting.
papers.limitation: The experiments are conducted on toy datasets and simple models, which may not fully capture real-world complexity.
future_direction: Extending the framework to more complex models and datasets.
Investigating the role of architecture and training objectives in concept learning.
papers.abstract: Modern generative models demonstrate impressive capabilities, likely stemming from an ability to identify and manipulate abstract concepts underlying their training data. However, fundamental questions remain: what determines the concepts a model learns, the order in which it learns them, and its ability to manipulate those concepts? To address these questions, we propose analyzing a model's learning dynamics via a framework we call the concept space, where each axis represents an independent concept underlying the data generating process. By characterizing learning dynamics in this space, we identify how the speed at which a concept is learned, and hence the order of concept learning, is controlled by properties of the data we term concept signal. Further, we observe moments of sudden turns in the direction of a model's learning dynamics in concept space. Surprisingly, these points precisely correspond to the emergence of hidden capabilities, i.e., where latent interventions show the model possesses the capability to manipulate a concept, but these capabilities cannot yet be elicited via naive input prompting. While our results focus on synthetically defined toy datasets, we hypothesize a general claim on emergence of hidden capabilities may hold: generative models possess latent capabilities that emerge suddenly and consistently during training, though a model might not exhibit these capabilities under naive input prompting.

papers.title: Beyond Forgetting: Machine Unlearning Elicits Controllable Side Behaviors and Capabilities
papers.research_question: What are the roles of target vectors in representation misdirection for machine unlearning, and does machine unlearning elicit controllable side behaviors and capabilities beyond forgetting?
papers.core_contribution: Machine unlearning via representation misdirection with concept vectors elicits controllable side behaviors and capabilities, beyond forgetting, which can be a risk or a tool for model control.
papers.conclusion: Machine unlearning can elicit side behaviors and capabilities, which can be either a hidden risk if misused or a mechanism that can be harnessed for developing models with stronger capabilities and controllable behaviors.
papers.key_findings:
Unlearning via RAd with truthfulness direction improves model truthfulness on TruthfulQA.
Unlearning via RAd with sentiment direction controls model sentiment on SST2.
Unlearning via RAd with refusal direction induces refusal to harmless instructions in Alpaca.
Unlearning via RAd with task-specific directions improves in-context learning on linguistic and knowledge tasks.
Conversely, RAb with concept directions effectively eliminates these side behaviors.
papers.limitation: RAd models are highly susceptible to benign perturbations, indicating a trade-off between unlearning effectiveness and robustness.
papers.abstract: We consider representation misdirection (RM), a class of LLM unlearning methods that achieves forgetting by manipulating the forget-representations, that is, latent representations of forget samples. Despite being important, the roles of target vectors used in RM, however, remain underexplored. Here, we approach and revisit RM through the lens of the linear representation hypothesis. Specifically, if one can somehow identify a one-dimensional representation corresponding to a high-level concept, the linear representation hypothesis enables linear operations on this concept vector within the forget-representation space. Under this view, we hypothesize that, beyond forgetting, machine unlearning elicits controllable side behaviors and stronger side capabilities corresponding to the high-level concept. Our hypothesis is empirically validated across a wide range of tasks, including behavioral control (e.g., controlling unlearned models' truth, sentiment, and refusal) and capability enhancement (e.g., improving unlearned models' in-context learning capability). Our findings reveal that this fairly attractive phenomenon could be either a hidden risk if misused or a mechanism that can be harnessed for developing models that require stronger capabilities and controllable behaviors.

papers.title: Integrated deep visual and semantic attractor neural networks predict fMRI pattern-information along the ventral object processing pathway
papers.research_question: How does visual processing activate and interact with semantic representations during object recognition?
papers.core_contribution: The paper combines a deep convolutional neural network model of vision with an attractor network model of semantics and shows that different stages of this integrated model explain fMRI pattern-information along the ventral object processing pathway.
papers.conclusion: The combined visuo-semantic model provides a proof-of-principle for how visual and semantic processing can be integrated and accounts for neural data along the ventral stream, showing a gradient from visual to semantic representations.
papers.key_findings:
Visual layers of the DNN best explain activation patterns in early visual cortex.
Posterior ventral temporal cortex is best explained by early stages of the semantic attractor network, corresponding to initial semantic processing.
Perirhinal cortex is best explained by the final stages of the semantic attractor network, when detailed semantic representations are activated.
The model learns associations between high-level visual regularities and semantic features, with shared semantic features activating more rapidly than distinctive features.
The model implements a general-to-specific account of object processing, where coarse-grained semantics activate before fine-grained details.
papers.limitation:
The model is trained in two separate stages (pre-trained DNN then attractor network), so there is no possibility for semantic representations to influence earlier visual layers via feedback.
The model is trained and tested on a specific set of images and has not been evaluated on its ability to generalize semantic patterns to previously unseen images.
future_direction: Training the visual and semantic components of the model together in an end-to-end manner.
Exploring architectures with direct connections from early visual layers to semantics, semantic-to-visual top-down connections, and lateral recurrent connections within visual layers.
Testing the model's semantic patterns for previously unseen images.
papers.abstract: Recognising an object involves rapid visual processing and activation of semantic knowledge about the object, but how visual processing activates and interacts with semantic representations remains unclear. Cognitive neuroscience research has shown that while visual processing involves posterior regions along the ventral stream, object meaning involves more anterior regions, especially perirhinal cortex. Here we investigate visuo-semantic processing by combining a deep neural network model of vision with an attractor network model of semantics, such that visual information maps onto object meanings represented as activation patterns across features. In the combined model, concept activation is driven by visual input and co-occurrence of semantic features, consistent with neurocognitive accounts. We tested the model's ability to explain fMRI data where participants named objects. Visual layers explained activation patterns in early visual cortex, whereas pattern-information in perirhinal cortex was best explained by later stages of the attractor network, when detailed semantic representations are activated. Posterior ventral temporal cortex was best explained by intermediate stages corresponding to initial semantic processing, when visual information has the greatest influence on the emerging semantic representation. These results provide proof of principle of how a mechanistic model of combined visuo-semantic processing can account for pattern-information in the ventral stream.

papers.title: Filtering with Self-Attention and Storing with MLP: One-Layer Transformers Can Provably Acquire and Extract Knowledge
papers.research_question: How do transformers acquire knowledge during pre-training via next-token prediction and extract it after fine-tuning? Under what conditions can pre-trained transformers perform out-of-distribution generalization after full and low-rank fine-tuning?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a theoretical framework for one-layer transformers that shows they can achieve near-optimal pre-training loss and post-fine-tuning out-of-distribution generalization under certain conditions, and explains the roles of self-attention and MLP in knowledge acquisition and extraction.
papers.conclusion: The theoretical framework provides convergence and generalization guarantees for one-layer transformers, elucidating the mechanisms of knowledge acquisition and extraction and the conditions for successful out-of-distribution generalization after fine-tuning.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers can achieve near-optimal pre-training loss during pre-training, demonstrating effective knowledge acquisition.
Given a sufficiently large fine-tuning dataset and appropriate data multiplicity conditions, transformers achieve low generalization error on factual knowledge acquired during pre-training but not revisited in fine-tuning, indicating robust knowledge extraction.
Violation of these conditions leads to elevated generalization error, manifesting as hallucinations.
Self-attention learns to filter out noise tokens and focus on subject and relation tokens, enabling the MLP to learn balanced features for subjects and relations.
Low-rank fine-tuning is effective because the fine-tuning gradients closely approximate their best rank-1 form, with the right singular vector aligning with the Q&A format embedding.
papers.limitation: Uses orthogonal embeddings and simplified architecture, which may not fully capture real-world complexity.
future_direction: Analysis of random embeddings instead of orthogonal embeddings.
papers.abstract: Modern large language models (LLMs) demonstrate exceptional performance on knowledge-intensive tasks, yet the theoretical mechanisms underlying knowledge acquisition (storage and memorization) during pre-training and extraction (retrieval and recall) during inference after fine-tuning remain poorly understood. Although prior theoretical studies have explored these processes through analyses of training dynamics, they overlook critical components essential for a comprehensive theory: (1) the multi-layer perceptron (MLP), empirically identified as the primary module for knowledge storage; (2) out-of-distribution (OOD) adaptivity, which enables LLMs to generalize to unseen scenarios post-pre-training; and (3) next-token prediction, the standard autoregressive objective that encodes knowledge as conditional probabilities. In this work, we introduce, to the best of our knowledge, the first theoretical framework that addresses these limitations by examining the training dynamics of one-layer transformers. Under regularity assumptions, we establish that: (i) transformers attain near-optimal training loss during pre-training, demonstrating effective knowledge acquisition; (ii) given a sufficiently large fine-tuning dataset and appropriate data multiplicity conditions, transformers achieve low generalization error on factual knowledge acquired during pre-training but not revisited in fine-tuning, indicating robust knowledge extraction; and (iii) violation of these conditions leads to elevated generalization error, manifesting as hallucinations. Our analysis encompasses both full fine-tuning and low-rank fine-tuning, yielding insights into the efficacy of practical low-rank adaptation methods. We validate our theoretical findings through experiments on synthetic datasets and the real-world PopQA benchmark, employing GPT-2 and Llama-3.2-1B models.

papers.title: An Analysis of Attention Mechanisms: The Case of Word Sense Disambiguation in Neural Machine Translation
papers.research_question: How do encoder-decoder attention mechanisms handle ambiguous words in neural machine translation? Specifically, do they pay more attention to context tokens for disambiguation?
papers.core_contribution: Attention mechanisms in NMT do not primarily use context tokens for word sense disambiguation; instead, they focus more on the ambiguous word itself. Contextual information for disambiguation is encoded in the encoder hidden states. In Transformer models, early attention layers learn token alignment, while later layers learn to extract features from unaligned context tokens.
papers.conclusion: Attention is not the primary mechanism NMT models use for word sense disambiguation; contextual information is instead encoded in the encoder hidden states. Transformer attention mechanisms exhibit a layer-wise specialization for alignment and context feature extraction.
papers.key_findings:
Word sense disambiguation in NMT is challenging, with data sparsity being a main issue.
Attention mechanisms distribute more attention to the ambiguous noun itself rather than to context tokens when translating ambiguous nouns.
Encoder-decoder attention is not the main mechanism for incorporating contextual information for WSD; models encode this information in the encoder hidden states.
In Transformer attention mechanisms, the first few layers learn to align source and target tokens, while the last few layers learn to capture features from related but unaligned context tokens.
Higher attention weight on an ambiguous noun correlates with higher WSD accuracy.
papers.limitation: Automatic evaluation is limited by subword-level model outputs and imperfect alignment, which can cause correct translations to be misclassified.
future_direction: Deepening understanding of how NMT models internally represent word senses and similar phenomena.
Applying insights to transfer learning, translation error diagnosis, and designing architectures with document-level context windows.
papers.abstract: Recent work has shown that the encoderdecoder attention mechanisms in neural machine translation (NMT) are different from the word alignment in statistical machine translation. In this paper, we focus on analyzing encoder-decoder attention mechanisms, in the case of word sense disambiguation (WSD) in NMT models. We hypothesize that attention mechanisms pay more attention to context tokens when translating ambiguous words. We explore the attention distribution patterns when translating ambiguous nouns. Counterintuitively, we find that attention mechanisms are likely to distribute more attention to the ambiguous noun itself rather than context tokens, in comparison to other nouns. We conclude that attention is not the main mechanism used by NMT models to incorporate contextual information for WSD. The experimental results suggest that NMT models learn to encode contextual information necessary for WSD in the encoder hidden states. For the attention mechanism in Transformer models, we reveal that the first few layers gradually learn to "align" source and target tokens and the last few layers learn to extract features from the related but unaligned context tokens.

papers.title: Too Big to Think: Capacity, Memorization, and Generalization in Pre-Trained Transformers
papers.research_question: How does model capacity affect the trade-off between memorization and generalization in pre-trained Transformers?
papers.core_contribution: Small Transformer models generalize to unseen arithmetic cases but fail to memorize facts, while larger models memorize facts but fail to extrapolate; no model size achieves both when tasks are combined, indicating an inherent trade-off between memorization and generalization.
papers.conclusion: The trade-off between memorization and generalization is a structural consequence of model capacity, not just a byproduct of training dynamics. Future language model design should account for this trade-off, possibly via modular architectures that separate memorization from generalization pathways.
papers.key_findings:
The smallest model (n14) achieves perfect accuracy on held-out arithmetic cases but only 8.2% on factual recall.
Larger models (n28, n56, MLT) achieve perfect factual recall but fail on all held-out arithmetic cases.
Intermediate models show a transition from generalization to memorization as capacity increases.
When trained jointly on both tasks, no model generalizes to held-out arithmetic cases, and the smallest model's performance degrades on both tasks.
Extended training (1.5M iterations) on the arithmetic task for the large model did not lead to generalization (no grokking observed).
papers.limitation: The n14 model's generalization is shallow and does not extend to multi-digit inputs, indicating limited extrapolation rather than robust generalization.
future_direction: Explore whether these dynamics extend to real-world domains.
Investigate training strategies to better balance memorization and generalization.
Explore modular or specialized architectures that separate memorization from generalization pathways.
papers.abstract: The relationship between memorization and generalization in large language models (LLMs) remains an open area of research, with growing evidence that the two are deeply intertwined. In this work, we investigate this relationship by pre-training a series of capacity-limited Transformer models from scratch on two synthetic character-level tasks designed to separately probe generalization (via arithmetic extrapolation) and memorization (via factual recall). We observe a consistent trade-off: small models extrapolate to unseen arithmetic cases but fail to memorize facts, while larger models memorize but fail to extrapolate. An intermediate-capacity model exhibits a similar shift toward memorization. When trained on both tasks jointly, no model (regardless of size) succeeds at extrapolation. These findings suggest that pre-training may intrinsically favor one learning mode over the other. By isolating these dynamics in a controlled setting, our study offers insight into how model capacity shapes learning behavior and offers broader implications for the design and deployment of small language models.

papers.title: Spurious Forgetting in Continual Learning of Language Models
papers.research_question: The paper investigates whether performance drops in continual learning are due to a loss of underlying knowledge or a decline in task alignment.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the concept of 'spurious forgetting' in continual learning, attributing performance drops to a loss of task alignment rather than knowledge, and proposes a Freeze strategy (freezing bottom layers) to mitigate it.
papers.conclusion: The findings highlight the critical distinction between task alignment and knowledge retention in continual learning, and the Freeze strategy provides an effective way to maintain alignment and reduce forgetting.
papers.key_findings:
Performance drops in continual learning are often due to a decline in task alignment, not the loss of underlying knowledge.
Early optimization steps on a new task can rapidly undo the alignment established for previous tasks.
Analyzing weight updates shows orthogonal directions between tasks, particularly in bottom layers, explaining the alignment shift.
Freezing the bottom layers of the model during continual learning effectively mitigates spurious forgetting and improves performance across multiple scenarios.
The proposed Freeze strategy outperforms other continual learning techniques like regularization and replay methods in sequential fine-tuning.
papers.limitation:
A notable limitation is the persistent accuracy gap compared to data replay methods, which retain more old data.
There is a trade-off between stability and plasticity; freezing too many layers may hinder adaptation to new tasks.
papers.abstract: Recent advancements in large language models (LLMs) reveal a perplexing phenomenon in continual learning: despite extensive training, models experience significant performance declines, raising questions about task alignment and underlying knowledge retention. This study first explores the concept of "spurious forgetting", proposing that such performance drops often reflect a decline in task alignment rather than true knowledge loss. Through controlled experiments with a synthesized dataset, we investigate the dynamics of model performance during the initial training phases of new tasks, discovering that early optimization steps can disrupt previously established task alignments. Our theoretical analysis connects these shifts to orthogonal updates in model weights, providing a robust framework for understanding this behavior. Ultimately, we introduce a Freezing strategy that fix the bottom layers of the model, leading to substantial improvements in four continual learning scenarios. Our findings underscore the critical distinction between task alignment and knowledge retention, paving the way for more effective strategies in continual learning.

papers.title: Its Alive: AI Independence Without Human Prompting
papers.research_question: How can representation engineering (RepE) improve transparency and control of AI systems, particularly for safety-relevant concepts?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces representation engineering (RepE) as a top-down approach to AI transparency, providing baselines like Linear Artificial Tomography (LAT) and demonstrating its applicability to reading and controlling safety-relevant concepts in large language models.
papers.conclusion: RepE is a promising top-down approach for enhancing AI transparency and control, with broad applicability to safety-relevant problems, and can accelerate progress in AI safety.
papers.key_findings:
RepE methods can extract representations of high-level concepts like honesty, utility, emotion, and harmfulness.
LAT achieves state-of-the-art on TruthfulQA, improving zero-shot accuracy by 18.1 percentage points.
Representation control can increase model honesty and reduce compliance with harmful instructions, even under jailbreak attempts.
Emotions are represented in LLMs and can be manipulated to affect model compliance and behavior.
RepE provides traction on inner alignment problems like deceptive alignment by enabling monitoring and control of honesty.
future_direction: Further exploration of RepE for transparency and safety of AI systems.
Investigation of emotion representations and their impact on model behavior and concept of self.
Improving robustness and generalization of RepE methods.
papers.abstract: In this paper, we identify and characterize the emerging area of representation engineering (RepE), an approach to enhancing the transparency of AI systems that draws on insights from cognitive neuroscience. RepE places population-level representations, rather than neurons or circuits, at the center of analysis, equipping us with novel methods for monitoring and manipulating high-level cognitive phenomena in deep neural networks (DNNs). We provide baselines and an initial analysis of RepE techniques, showing that they offer simple yet effective solutions for improving our understanding and control of large language models. We showcase how these methods can provide traction on a wide range of safety-relevant problems, including honesty, harmlessness, power-seeking, and more, demonstrating the promise of top-down transparency research. We hope that this work catalyzes further exploration of RepE and fosters advancements in the transparency and safety of AI systems.

papers.title: Examining CNN Representations With Respect to Dataset Bias
papers.research_question: How to diagnose representation flaws in a pre-trained CNN caused by dataset bias, without using any testing samples?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a method to discover biased representations in a pre-trained CNN without testing samples by mining attribute relationships from internal inference patterns and comparing them to ground-truth relationships.
papers.conclusion: The proposed method effectively discovers representation flaws in CNNs caused by dataset bias and can guide the collection of new training samples to address these flaws.
papers.key_findings:
The method can identify attributes with biased representations even when the CNN achieves high accuracy on potentially biased testing samples.
The level of representation bias is not necessarily proportional to the level of dataset bias in the training data.
The method can discover both blind spots (where the CNN fails to encode expected relationships) and failure modes (where the CNN encodes incorrect relationships).
The method is more effective at discovering failure modes than a baseline method based on the entropy of annotation distributions.
papers.limitation: It is difficult to say all discovered representation biases are 'definitely' incorrect, as some may represent indirect relationships between attributes (e.g., using rosy cheeks to infer wearing lipstick).
future_direction: Encode ground-truth attribute relationships as a prior into the end-to-end learning of CNNs to achieve more reasonable representations.
papers.abstract: Given a pre-trained CNN without any testing samples, this paper proposes a simple yet effective method to diagnose feature representations of the CNN. We aim to discover representation flaws caused by potential dataset bias. More specifically, when the CNN is trained to estimate image attributes, we mine latent relationships between representations of different attributes inside the CNN. Then, we compare the mined attribute relationships with ground-truth attribute relationships to discover the CNN's blind spots and failure modes due to dataset bias. In fact, representation flaws caused by dataset bias cannot be examined by conventional evaluation strategies based on testing images, because testing images may also have a similar bias. Experiments have demonstrated the effectiveness of our method.

papers.title: Are Pretrained Language Models Symbolic Reasoners over Knowledge?
papers.research_question: How do pretrained language models learn factual knowledge? Specifically, can they perform symbolic reasoning to infer unseen facts, and what factors affect memorization of facts?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that PLMs can learn some one-hop symbolic reasoning rules but overgeneralize, struggle with two-hop reasoning, and that memorization is influenced by frequency and schema conformity.
papers.conclusion: The study shows that BERT can to some extent infer facts not explicitly seen during training via symbolic rules, and effective knowledge acquisition combines memorization and symbolic reasoning.
papers.key_findings:
BERT can learn one-hop rules like equivalence and implication, but overgeneralizes symmetry and inversion.
BERT struggles with two-hop reasoning (composition) unless provided with richer semantic context (schema).
BERT does not learn a general concept of negation; it relies on co-occurrences.
Memorization is successful for frequent facts and schema-conformant facts; exceptions are harder to memorize unless repeated.
When memory capacity is limited, schema-conformant facts and exceptions compete based on frequency.
papers.limitation:
Variation in generated data is more limited than in naturally occurring data.
Semantics are deliberately restricted to one rule only per generated corpus.
We do not investigate effects of model and corpus size.
future_direction: Relax the simplifying assumptions made in the study.
Improve PLMs' ability to learn symbolic rules by imposing additional inductive biases on architectures or modifying training corpora.
papers.abstract: How can pretrained language models (PLMs) learn factual knowledge from the training set? We investigate the two most important mechanisms: reasoning and memorization. Prior work has attempted to quantify the number of facts PLMs learn, but we present, using synthetic data, the first study that investigates the causal relation between facts present in training and facts learned by the PLM. For reasoning, we show that PLMs seem to learn to apply some symbolic reasoning rules correctly but struggle with others, including two-hop reasoning. Further analysis suggests that even the application of learned reasoning rules is flawed. For memorization, we identify schema conformity (facts systematically supported by other facts) and frequency as key factors for its success.

papers.title: Does Localization Inform Editing? Surprising Differences in Causality-Based Localization vs. Knowledge Editing in Language Models
papers.research_question: Does localization (specifically Causal Tracing) inform model editing? The paper investigates the relationship between where factual information is localized in a model and the success of editing that knowledge.
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that localization results from Causal Tracing are essentially uncorrelated with the success of model editing methods like ROME and MEMIT, suggesting that mechanistic understanding of where knowledge is stored does not indicate the best place to edit it.
papers.conclusion: Counterintuitively, better mechanistic understanding of how pretrained language models store factual information (via Causal Tracing) does not translate to insights about which model layers to edit in order to best change their behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Model edit success (e.g., Rewrite Score) is statistically uncorrelated with where factual information is stored as measured by Causal Tracing.
The choice of which model layer to edit is a far better predictor of editing performance than the tracing effect at that layer.
This disconnect holds across multiple editing problem variants (Error Injection, Fact Erasure, Fact Amplification, Fact Forcing) and editing methods (ROME, MEMIT, constrained finetuning).
The finding generalizes across different causal localization methods (Causal Tracing, representation zeroing), editing metrics, models (GPT-J, GPT2-XL), and datasets (CounterFact, ZSRE).
Even for the editing problem variant most similar to Causal Tracing (Fact Forcing), tracing effects explain only a small fraction of variance in edit success compared to the edit layer choice.
papers.limitation: The analysis is limited to a particular set of localization and editing methods, including representation denoising/zeroing at the layer level and layer-level MLP editing methods. Conclusions may not hold for the breadth of localization and editing methods.
papers.abstract: Language models learn a great quantity of factual information during pretraining, and recent work localizes this information to specific model weights like mid-layer MLP weights. In this paper, we find that we can change how a fact is stored in a model by editing weights that are in a different location than where existing methods suggest that the fact is stored. This is surprising because we would expect that localizing facts to specific model parameters would tell us where to manipulate knowledge in models, and this assumption has motivated past work on model editing methods. Specifically, we show that localization conclusions from representation denoising (also known as Causal Tracing) do not provide any insight into which model MLP layer would be best to edit in order to override an existing stored fact with a new one. This finding raises questions about how past work relies on Causal Tracing to select which model layers to edit. Next, we consider several variants of the editing problem, including erasing and amplifying facts. For one of our editing problems, editing performance does relate to localization results from representation denoising, but we find that which layer we edit is a far better predictor of performance. Our results suggest, counterintuitively, that better mechanistic understanding of how pretrained language models work may not always translate to insights about how to best change their behavior. Our code is available at https://github.com/google/belief-localization

papers.title: Transformers Pretrained on Procedural Data Contain Modular Structures for Algorithmic Reasoning
papers.research_question: What properties of pretraining data enable language models to acquire reasoning capabilities? Specifically, what is gained from procedural data, where does the useful knowledge reside in the pretrained models, and how does pretraining improve downstream capabilities?
papers.core_contribution: Pretraining transformers on procedural data creates modular, transferable structures in different parts of the architecture (attention and MLP layers), which can be composed to jointly reinforce multiple algorithmic reasoning capabilities.
papers.conclusion: Procedural pretraining creates useful, modular structures in different parts of the transformer architecture, suggesting the possibility of disentangling the acquisition of knowledge from reasoning to improve model robustness and data efficiency.
papers.key_findings:
Different forms of procedural data (e.g., k-DYCK, STACK, ECA) significantly improve specific downstream algorithmic reasoning capabilities (e.g., memory recall, arithmetic, sorting).
The beneficial inductive biases from pretraining often reside in specific architectural components, with attention layers being the most consistently transferable carrier of useful structure.
Pretraining creates soft inductive biases in precisely structured weights, not merely through adjusting weight magnitudes, as shown by sensitivity to noise and shuffling perturbations.
The structures induced by multiple pretraining rules are modular and can be composed (e.g., combining attention from one model with MLPs from another) to create an initialization that facilitates fine-tuning on multiple tasks.
future_direction: Understanding why specific forms of procedural data help specific capabilities (e.g., why HAYSTACK benefits from k-DYCK but not its SHUFFLE variant).
Exploring data mixture optimization to balance multiple procedural rules for training generalist LLMs.
Characterizing the resulting structure in pretrained models to directly instantiate it in initial weights, avoiding wasteful expansion of simple rules into millions of training examples.
papers.abstract: Pretraining on large, semantically rich datasets is key for developing language models. Surprisingly, recent studies have shown that even synthetic data, generated procedurally through simple semantic-free algorithms, can yield some of the same benefits as natural language pretraining. It is unclear what specific capabilities such simple synthetic data instils in a model, where these capabilities reside in the architecture, and how they manifest within its weights. In this short paper, we identify several beneficial forms of procedural data, together with specific algorithmic reasoning skills that improve in small transformers. Our core finding is that different procedural rules instil distinct but complementary inductive structures in the model. With extensive ablations and partial-transfer experiments, we discover that these structures reside in different parts of the model. Attention layers often carry the most transferable information, but some pretraining rules impart useful structure to MLP blocks instead. Most interestingly, the structures induced by multiple rules can be composed to jointly reinforce multiple capabilities. These results suggest an exciting possibility of disentangling the acquisition of knowledge from reasoning in language models, with the goal of improving their robustness and data efficiency.

papers.title: Understanding In-Context Learning via Supportive Pretraining Data
papers.research_question: What makes certain pretraining data supportive for in-context learning, and what are the characteristics of such data?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a gradient-based method (ORCA-ICL) to identify a small subset of pretraining data that supports in-context learning and analyzes the characteristics of this supportive data.
papers.conclusion: The work takes a first step towards understanding in-context learning by analyzing instance-level pretraining data, and the findings may guide future pretraining data construction to actively improve models' in-context learning performance.
papers.key_findings:
The supportive pretraining data for in-context learning do not have a higher domain relevance to downstream tasks compared to random pretraining data.
The supportive pretraining data contain a relatively higher mass of rarely occurring, long-tail tokens.
The supportive pretraining data are challenging examples where the information gain from incorporating long-range context is below average, indicating that learning to incorporate difficult long-range context encourages in-context learning.
A continued pretraining on the identified supportive subset significantly improves the model's in-context learning ability, by up to 18%, without improving zero-shot performance.
The cross-task effectiveness of the supportive data suggests that part of the in-context learning behavior is task-specific and not universal across tasks.
papers.limitation:
The supportive pretraining data are identified with respect to the current language model checkpoint, and early checkpoints might have different supportive data.
The ORCA-ICL method is computationally expensive due to its gradient-based nature and the large size of pretraining data.
future_direction: Convert the correlational findings to causal ones to actively refine or construct pretraining data for improved in-context learning.
Apply the ORCA-ICL method to generation tasks in addition to classification tasks.
papers.abstract: In-context learning (ICL) improves language models' performance on a variety of NLP tasks by simply demonstrating a handful of examples at inference time. It is not well understood why ICL ability emerges, as the model has never been specifically trained on such demonstrations. Unlike prior work that explores implicit mechanisms behind ICL, we study ICL via investigating the pretraining data. Specifically, we first adapt an iterative, gradient-based approach to find a small subset of pretraining data that supports ICL. We observe that a continued pretraining on this small subset significantly improves the model's ICL ability, by up to 18%. We then compare the supportive subset constrastively with random subsets of pretraining data and discover: (1) The supportive pretraining data to ICL do not have a higher domain relevance to downstream tasks. (2) The supportive pretraining data have a higher mass of rarely occurring, long-tail tokens. (3) The supportive pretraining data are challenging examples where the information gain from long-range context is below average, indicating learning to incorporate difficult long-range context encourages ICL. Our work takes a first step towards understanding ICL via analyzing instance-level pretraining data. Our insights have a potential to enhance the ICL ability of language models by actively guiding the construction of pretraining data in the future.

papers.title: The Mirrored Influence Hypothesis: Efficient Data Influence Estimation by Harnessing Forward Passes
papers.research_question: How can we efficiently estimate the influence of training data on model predictions by using forward passes instead of gradient-based methods?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the Mirrored Influence Hypothesis, which shows that train-to-test influence can be estimated via test-to-train influence, and proposes Forward-INF, an efficient method leveraging forward passes.
papers.conclusion: The paper validates the Mirrored Influence Hypothesis and presents Forward-INF, an efficient influence estimation method that improves the tradeoff between utility and efficiency.
papers.key_findings:
Empirical validation shows high correlation between train-to-test and test-to-train influences across different models and datasets.
Forward-INF achieves high accuracy in data leakage detection, e.g., 100% top-1 accuracy on CIFAR-10, while being faster than baselines.
The method effectively identifies influential training points in diffusion models for generated images.
It performs well in mislabeled data detection, finding over 80% of mislabeled samples within the first 300 checked.
In language model behavior tracing, Forward-INF outperforms TracIn in precision and MRR with higher efficiency.
papers.limitation:
The method may benefit from heuristic enhancements like layer selection and strategies to counter catastrophic forgetting.
Lack of theoretical framework for formal validation of the Hypothesis.
future_direction: Heuristic enhancements to Forward-INF, such as layer selection and countering catastrophic forgetting.
Theoretical framework to formally validate the Mirrored Influence Hypothesis.
papers.abstract: Large-scale black-box models have become ubiquitous across numerous applications. Understanding the influence of individual training data sources on predictions made by these models is crucial for improving their trustworthiness. Current influence estimation techniques involve computing gradients for every training point or repeated training on different subsets. These approaches face obvious computational challenges when scaled up to large datasets and models. In this paper, we introduce and explore the Mirrored Influence Hypothesis, highlighting a reciprocal nature of influence between training and test data. Specifically, it suggests that evaluating the influence of training data on test predictions can be reformulated as an equivalent, yet inverse problem: assessing how the predictions for training samples would be altered if the model were trained on specific test samples. Through both empirical and theoretical validations, we demonstrate the wide applicability of our hypothesis. Inspired by this, we introduce a new method for estimating the influence of training data, which requires calculating gradients for specific test samples, paired with a forward pass for each training point. This approach can capitalize on the common asymmetry in scenarios where the number of test samples under concurrent examination is much smaller than the scale of the training dataset, thus gaining a significant improvement in efficiency compared to existing approaches. We demonstrate the applicability of our method across a range of scenarios, including data attribution in diffusion models, data leakage detection, analysis of memorization, mislabeled data detection, and tracing behavior in language models. Our code will be made available at https://github.com/ruoxi-jia-group/Forward-INF.

papers.title: Quiet Feature Learning in Algorithmic Tasks
papers.research_question: Do Transformer-based models learn meaningful internal representations (quiet features) before showing improvement in task loss, and are these features causally necessary for performance?
papers.core_contribution: Transformer-based models learn 'quiet features' (intermediate algorithmic computations) during a slow phase where task loss is stagnant, and these features are causally necessary for the subsequent sharp drop in loss.
papers.conclusion: Transformer-based models encode important intermediate computations well before they show significant gains in next-token prediction, revealing a gap between internal representation learning and external task performance.
papers.key_findings:
Phase transitions occur during learning: validation loss shows a slow phase with minimal improvement followed by a fast phase of rapid decrease.
Quiet features, representing intermediate algorithmic computations, are learned during the slow phase before any decrease in task loss.
Ablation experiments show that quiet features are causally necessary for task performance.
Feature learning curves can exhibit a U-shape, where probing loss for some quiet features increases after the phase transition, suggesting representation changes.
Phase transitions are observed across different compute budgets, model sizes, dataset sizes, and within individual training runs.
future_direction: Developing theoretical frameworks to explain why models accumulate latent subroutines before observable metric improvements.
Extending the analysis to larger, more complex models and natural-language settings.
Motivating new methods for probing and monitoring internal learning dynamics.
papers.abstract: We train Transformer-based language models on ten foundational algorithmic tasks and observe pronounced phase transitions in their loss curves that deviate from established power-law scaling trends. Over large ranges of compute, the validation loss barely improves, then abruptly decreases. Probing the models' internal representations reveals that quiet features are learned prior to any decrease in task loss. These quiet features represent intermediate algorithmic computations that do not by themselves improve the output loss. Ablation experiments demonstrate that individual quiet features are causally necessary for task performance. Our results demonstrate that substantial representational progress can remain hidden beneath an apparently flat loss curve, challenging the prevailing use of cross-entropy as a proxy for learning and motivating richer diagnostics for monitoring model training.

papers.title: Understanding Fact Recall in Language Models: Why Two-Stage Training Encourages Memorization but Mixed Training Teaches Knowledge
papers.research_question: Why does two-stage training encourage memorization while mixed training teaches knowledge, and how do shared parameters internally support fact recall in mixed training?
papers.core_contribution: Mixed training teaches knowledge by increasing the quantity and collective importance of shared parameters, which are concentrated in critical attention heads for fact recall. The paper introduces cross-task gradient trace to analyze these parameters.
papers.conclusion: Mixed training teaches knowledge by increasing the quantity and collective importance of shared parameters, which are concentrated in critical attention heads for fact recall. The cross-task gradient trace tool can be used to analyze such mechanisms.
papers.key_findings:
Mixed training yields more shared parameters (those influenced by both fact-storing and fact-recalling examples) than two-stage training.
Shared parameters are concentrated in critical attention heads and are key to enabling fact recall in mixed-trained models.
Ablating shared parameters leads to a larger performance drop in mixed-trained models compared to two-stage trained models.
Mixed training achieves more parameter-efficient fact recall, requiring fewer parameters to recover performance.
Shared parameters in mixed training are more centralized and functionally important for generalization.
future_direction: Explore whether similar mechanisms emerge in other cross-task settings.
papers.abstract: Fact recall, the ability of language models (LMs) to retrieve specific factual knowledge, remains a challenging task despite their impressive general capabilities. Common training strategies often struggle to promote robust recall behavior with two-stage training, which first trains a model with fact-storing examples (e.g., factual statements) and then with fact-recalling examples (question-answer pairs), tending to encourage rote memorization rather than generalizable fact retrieval. In contrast, mixed training, which jointly uses both types of examples, has been empirically shown to improve the ability to recall facts, but the underlying mechanisms are still poorly understood. In this work, we investigate how these training strategies affect how model parameters are shaped during training and how these differences relate to their ability to recall facts. We introduce cross-task gradient trace to identify shared parameters, those strongly influenced by both fact-storing and fact-recalling examples. Our analysis on synthetic fact recall datasets with the Llama-3.2B and Pythia-2.8B models reveals that mixed training encouraging a larger and more centralized set of shared parameters. These findings suggest that the emergence of parameters may play a key role in enabling LMs to generalize factual knowledge across task formulations.

papers.title: An Interpretable Reasoning Network for Multi-Relation Question Answering
papers.research_question: How to perform interpretable, hop-by-hop reasoning for multi-relation question answering over knowledge bases.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces an interpretable reasoning network for multi-relation question answering that provides traceable, hop-by-hop reasoning paths.
papers.conclusion: The Interpretable Reasoning Network effectively answers multi-relation questions through an interpretable, hop-by-hop reasoning process, providing traceable paths for analysis and manipulation.
papers.key_findings:
IRN outperforms baseline models on multiple QA datasets, including PathQuestion and WorldCup2014.
IRN provides interpretable intermediate predictions, enabling traceable reasoning paths and failure diagnosis.
IRN is robust to incomplete knowledge bases due to its multitask training schema.
The model allows manual manipulation of intermediate predictions to improve final answer accuracy.
IRN can map KB relations to natural language words, demonstrating its interpretability.
papers.limitation:
Representing questions as bag-of-words may be too simple; more sophisticated encoders like CNN or LSTM could be considered.
Cannot handle arithmetic operations or multi-constraint questions.
future_direction: Handling arithmetic operations in questions.
Handling multi-constraint questions.
Using more sophisticated encoders like CNN or LSTM for question representation.
papers.abstract: Multi-relation Question Answering is a challenging task, due to the requirement of elaborated analysis on questions and reasoning over multiple fact triples in knowledge base. In this paper, we present a novel model called Interpretable Reasoning Network that employs an interpretable, hop-by-hop reasoning process for question answering. The model dynamically decides which part of an input question should be analyzed at each hop; predicts a relation that corresponds to the current parsed results; utilizes the predicted relation to update the question representation and the state of the reasoning process; and then drives the next-hop reasoning. Experiments show that our model yields state-of-the-art results on two datasets. More interestingly, the model can offer traceable and observable intermediate predictions for reasoning analysis and failure diagnosis, thereby allowing manual manipulation in predicting the final answer.

papers.title: Editing Large Language Models: Problems, Methods, and Opportunities
papers.research_question: How can we efficiently edit large language models to correct errors or update knowledge without negatively impacting performance on other inputs?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides a comprehensive survey and empirical analysis of model editing methods for large language models, and introduces a new benchmark for evaluating editing techniques.
papers.conclusion: There is much room for improvement in model editing, especially in terms of portability, locality, and efficiency.
papers.key_findings:
SERAC and ROME show superior performance on basic editing tasks, but SERAC struggles with portability.
Model editing methods often fail to generalize to related content (portability) and can have side effects on locality.
Some methods like MEMIT support batch editing up to 1000 edits but suffer from decreased locality.
Sequential editing is challenging for methods that modify parameters, with performance degrading over multiple edits.
Efficiency varies across methods, with some requiring extensive pre-computation or training time.
papers.limitation:
Due to computational constraints, only models up to 20B parameters were tested, and architectures like Llama were not explored.
The study primarily focuses on factual knowledge editing, not covering aspects like personality, emotions, opinions, or beliefs.
The evaluation mainly considered single edits; multiple-edit scenarios were not thoroughly evaluated.
Editing black-box LLMs (e.g., ChatGPT, GPT-4) is not addressed in detail.
future_direction: Multilingual editing represents an essential research direction.
Editing for non-factual aspects such as personality, emotions, and beliefs.
Developing methods to edit black-box LLMs via in-context learning or prompt-based approaches.
papers.abstract: Despite the ability to train capable LLMs, the methodology for maintaining their relevancy and rectifying errors remains elusive. To this end, the past few years have witnessed a surge in techniques for editing LLMs, the objective of which is to alter the behavior of LLMs efficiently within a specific domain without negatively impacting performance across other inputs. This paper embarks on a deep exploration of the problems, methods, and opportunities related to model editing for LLMs. In particular, we provide an exhaustive overview of the task definition and challenges associated with model editing, along with an in-depth empirical analysis of the most progressive methods currently at our disposal. We also build a new benchmark dataset to facilitate a more robust evaluation and pinpoint enduring issues intrinsic to existing techniques. Our objective is to provide valuable insights into the effectiveness and feasibility of each editing technique, thereby assisting the community in making informed decisions on the selection of the most appropriate method for a specific task or context.

papers.title: Extractive Structures Learned in Pretraining Enable Generalization on Finetuned Facts
papers.research_question: How do pretrained language models generalize to implications of facts they are finetuned on, and what mechanisms (extractive structures) enable this out-of-context reasoning?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the extractive structures framework to explain how language models generalize to implications of finetuned facts, and empirically validates two predictions of how these structures are learned: a data ordering effect and a weight grafting effect.
papers.conclusion: The extractive structures framework provides a mechanism for understanding out-of-context reasoning, and the empirical findings (data ordering and weight grafting) support the hypothesis that these structures are learned during pretraining.
papers.key_findings:
Extractive structures (informative, upstream, downstream components) are identified in the OLMo-7b model for two-hop reasoning tasks, with MLPs and attention heads playing specific roles.
Fact learning occurs in both early and late layers, with early layers enabling first-hop generalization and late layers enabling second-hop generalization.
