This addressing scheme maintains for each memory cell two separate vectors, content and address vectors. This allows the D-NTM to learn a wide variety of location-based addressing strategies including both linear and nonlinear ones. We implement the D-NTM with both continuous, differentiable and discrete, non-differentiable read/write mechanisms. We investigate the mechanisms and effects of learning to read and write into a memory through experiments on Facebook bAbI tasks using both a feedforward and GRUcontroller. The D-NTM is evaluated on a set of Facebook bAbI tasks and shown to outperform NTM and LSTM baselines. We have done extensive analysis of our model and different variations of NTM on bAbI task. We also provide further experimental results on sequential pMNIST, Stanford Natural Language Inference, associative recall and copy tasks.

papers.title: Sudden Drops in the Loss: Syntax Acquisition, Phase Transitions, and Simplicity Bias in MLMs
papers.research_question: How does syntactic attention structure (SAS) emerge during training of masked language models, and what is its causal role in the development of grammatical capabilities?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that syntactic attention structure (SAS) emerges abruptly during training and is necessary for grammatical capabilities; briefly suppressing SAS early in training can improve model quality by allowing an alternative strategy to emerge.
papers.conclusion: Developmental analysis of training dynamics is crucial for understanding model behavior, and SAS represents a simplicity bias that can be manipulated to improve training.
papers.key_findings:
SAS emerges abruptly during training in a phase transition called the structure onset.
The structure onset precedes and is necessary for the capabilities onset, which marks improvements in grammatical capabilities.
Suppressing SAS throughout training prevents the development of grammatical capabilities.
Briefly suppressing SAS early in training improves model quality and accelerates convergence.
There exists an alternative strategy that competes with SAS, and suppressing SAS allows this alternative strategy to emerge earlier.
papers.abstract: Most interpretability research in NLP focuses on understanding the behavior and features of a fully trained model. However, certain insights into model behavior may only be accessible by observing the trajectory of the training process. We present a case study of syntax acquisition in masked language models (MLMs) that demonstrates how analyzing the evolution of interpretable artifacts throughout training deepens our understanding of emergent behavior. In particular, we study Syntactic Attention Structure (SAS), a naturally emerging property of MLMs wherein specific Transformer heads tend to focus on specific syntactic relations. We identify a brief window in pretraining when models abruptly acquire SAS, concurrent with a steep drop in loss. This breakthrough precipitates the subsequent acquisition of linguistic capabilities. We then examine the causal role of SAS by manipulating SAS during training, and demonstrate that SAS is necessary for the development of grammatical capabilities. We further find that SAS competes with other beneficial traits during training, and that briefly suppressing SAS improves model quality. These findings offer an interpretation of a real-world example of both simplicity bias and breakthrough training dynamics.

papers.title: Study of Pretraining Bias and Frequencies
papers.research_question: How do pretraining term frequencies and pretraining bias impact the performance of language models in an in-context learning setting?
papers.core_contribution: The performance of language models in in-context learning is significantly influenced by the pretraining frequencies of terms in demonstrations, and models can overcome pretraining bias when provided with more demonstrations.
papers.conclusion: Pretraining data has a significant impact on in-context learning performance, and language models can overcome pretraining bias when provided with more demonstrations that illustrate the correct input-output mapping.
papers.key_findings:
Model performance on arithmetic tasks is positively correlated with the pretraining frequency of the numbers involved.
Using high-frequency numbers in few-shot demonstrations can improve task performance.
With random demonstrations, model performance initially relies on pretraining bias but decreases with more shots as the model starts to learn the input-output mapping.
In adversarial demonstrations (e.g., prompting for subtraction when biased towards addition), the model can overcome its pretraining bias as the number of shots increases.
Reinforcement learning finetuning provides only minor improvements, with primary learning stemming from pretraining and supervised finetuning.
future_direction: Improving the learning capabilities of language models in low-frequency environments.
Studying the difference between embeddings of high-frequency and low-frequency numbers.
Building hybrid applications that use language models for high-frequency computations and external APIs for low-frequency environments.
papers.abstract: Usage of language models in an in-context learning environment has been adapted for a wide range of tasks. Recent works have showcased the impact of pretraining data on the in-context performance of language models. In this work, we experiment with numbers having high and low frequencies in the pretraining data to understand the impact of term frequencies on the model's performance. We also experiment with random and adversarial demonstrations to understand the pretraining bias present in the model. Through these experiments, we showcase the importance of pretraining frequencies of the numbers present in the demonstrations and explain how highly frequent terms can be used in the demonstrations to achieve better task performance. Moreover, we also show the impact of pretraining bias on the model's performance and explain how the model overcomes this bias with more demonstrations.

papers.title: Influence Dynamics and Stagewise Data Attribution
papers.research_question: How does the influence of training data on model behavior change dynamically over the course of training, challenging the static view of influence functions?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a framework for stagewise data attribution based on singular learning theory, showing that influence of training data changes dynamically during learning, with non-monotonic changes and peaks at developmental phase transitions.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that influence is dynamic and stagewise, challenging the static view of influence functions, and proposes stagewise data attribution as a new framework for understanding data impact during learning.
papers.key_findings:
Influence is not static but changes non-monotonically over training, including sign flips and sharp peaks at developmental transitions.
In a toy model of hierarchical feature learning, dynamic shifts in influence correspond to the model's progressive learning of semantic hierarchy.
In language models, token-level influence changes align with known developmental stages, such as the formation of induction circuits.
The Bayesian Influence Function (BIF) is a suitable tool for measuring influence in singular models, as it is Hessian-free and well-defined throughout training.
Stagewise data attribution provides a new perspective on when and why data matters during learning, moving beyond static attribution.
papers.limitation: The Bayesian Influence Function requires careful hyperparameter tuning for accurate estimation, as shown in the hyperparameter sweep.
papers.abstract: Current training data attribution (TDA) methods treat the influence one sample has on another as static, but neural networks learn in distinct stages that exhibit changing patterns of influence. In this work, we introduce a framework for stagewise data attribution grounded in singular learning theory. We predict that influence can change non-monotonically, including sign flips and sharp peaks at developmental transitions. We first validate these predictions analytically and empirically in a toy model, showing that dynamic shifts in influence directly map to the model's progressive learning of a semantic hierarchy. Finally, we demonstrate these phenomena at scale in language models, where token-level influence changes align with known developmental stages.

papers.title: Language Models Are Capable of Metacognitive Monitoring and Control of Their Internal Activations
papers.research_question: Can LLMs accurately monitor and control their internal neural activations? Why can they report some intermediate steps but not others?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a neurofeedback paradigm to quantify metacognitive abilities in LLMs, showing they can report and control internal activations along certain axes, with performance depending on interpretability, variance, and context.
papers.conclusion: LLMs have limited metacognitive abilities to monitor and control their internal activations, which raises important considerations for AI safety and alignment.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs can report neural activations along target axes, with performance improving with more in-context examples and being better for semantically interpretable axes.
LLMs can explicitly and implicitly control neural activations, with explicit control being stronger and effects increasing with model size and depth.
Control effects are stronger for axes with semantic interpretability and those explaining more variance.
The axes that can be reported and controlled span a low-dimensional 'metacognitive space'.
Metacognitive abilities have implications for AI safety, as models might evade neural-based oversight.
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to instruction-fine-tuned models and may not generalize to base models.
The neurofeedback paradigm assumes the model can understand the task, which may not hold for all models or tasks.
future_direction: Extend the neurofeedback paradigm to more models and datasets.
Investigate the neural mechanisms underlying metacognitive control in LLMs.
Explore applications in AI safety, such as developing better oversight methods.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can sometimes report the strategies they actually use to solve tasks, yet at other times seem unable to recognize those strategies that govern their behavior. This suggests a limited degree of metacognition - the capacity to monitor one's own cognitive processes for subsequent reporting and self-control. Metacognition enhances LLMs' capabilities in solving complex tasks but also raises safety concerns, as models may obfuscate their internal processes to evade neural-activation-based oversight (e.g., safety detector). Given society's increased reliance on these models, it is critical that we understand their metacognitive abilities. To address this, we introduce a neuroscience-inspired neurofeedback paradigm that uses in-context learning to quantify metacognitive abilities of LLMs to report and control their activation patterns. We demonstrate that their abilities depend on several factors: the number of in-context examples provided, the semantic interpretability of the neural activation direction (to be reported/controlled), and the variance explained by that direction. These directions span a "metacognitive space" with dimensionality much lower than the model's neural space, suggesting LLMs can monitor only a small subset of their neural activations. Our paradigm provides empirical evidence to quantify metacognition in LLMs, with significant implications for AI safety (e.g., adversarial attack and defense).

papers.title: Retentive or Forgetful? Diving into the Knowledge Memorizing Mechanism of Language Models
papers.research_question: What are the memorizing dynamics of language models, and how does pre-training affect their memory ability?
papers.core_contribution: Pre-training transforms language models from forgetful to retentive by enabling long-term memory formation, influenced by knowledge relevance and diversity.
papers.conclusion: Vanilla language models are forgetful, pre-training leads to retentive models, and knowledge relevance and diversification significantly influence memory formation.
papers.key_findings:
Vanilla language models are forgetful with short memory duration and limited capacity.
Pre-trained language models are retentive and can gradually memorize knowledge through repetitive learning.
Pre-training is crucial for developing long-term memory ability in language models.
There is memory competition between highly relevant knowledge types in pre-trained models.
Lack of knowledge diversity causes memory collapse in early learning stages.
future_direction: Investigate the underlying reasons for the forgetful-retentive transition during pre-training.
Explore other critical factors affecting memorization beyond pre-training and diversity.
Compare memorization mechanisms between language models and the human brain.
papers.abstract: Memory is one of the most essential cognitive functions serving as a repository of world knowledge and episodes of activities. In recent years, large-scale pre-trained language models have shown remarkable memorizing ability. On the contrary, vanilla neural networks without pre-training have been long observed suffering from the catastrophic forgetting problem. To investigate such a retentive-forgetful contradiction and understand the memory mechanism of language models, we conduct thorough experiments by controlling the target knowledge types, the learning strategies and the learning schedules. We find that: 1) Vanilla language models are forgetful; 2) Pre-training leads to retentive language models; 3) Knowledge relevance and diversification significantly influence the memory formation. These conclusions are useful for understanding the abilities of pre-trained language models and shed light on designing and evaluating new learning and inference algorithms of language models.

papers.title: Question-Answering with Grammatically-Interpretable Representations
papers.research_question: Can internal representations in a neural network trained on a question-answering task be interpreted using linguistic concepts (symbols as lexical-semantic meanings and roles as grammatical roles) without explicit grammatical supervision?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the Tensor Product Recurrent Network (TPRN), an architecture that learns interpretable internal representations (symbols and roles) while performing comparably to a state-of-the-art model on the SQuAD question-answering task.
papers.conclusion: The TPRN model learns internal representations interpretable as encoding abstract grammatical concepts without exposure to grammatically annotated data, lending plausibility to the hypothesis that such representations are learned in human language acquisition.
papers.key_findings:
The learned symbols correspond to lexical-semantic meanings, with words assigned to the same symbol being semantically related.
The learned roles correspond to abstract grammatical roles (e.g., determiner, predicate, plural, wh-operator restrictor, subject/agent vs. object/patient).
The model's learned representations can correct some errors made by a standard part-of-speech tagger (Stanford Tagger).
The model distinguishes between different meanings of polysemous words (e.g., 'who') via different symbol selections.
Output errors can sometimes be attributed to identifiable errors in internal representation, such as misassigning a symbol.
future_direction: Scaling up the model to full-blown Tensor Product Representation architectures.
Further developing error analysis to attribute output errors to internal misrepresentations.
papers.abstract: We introduce an architecture, the Tensor Product RecurrentNetwork (TPRN). In our application of TPRN, internal representations—learned by end-to-end optimization in a deep neural network performing a textual question-answering(QA) task—can be interpreted using basic concepts from linguistic theory. No performance penalty need be paid for this increased interpretability: the proposed model performs comparably to a state-of-the-art system on the SQuAD QA task.The internal representation which is interpreted is a Tensor Product Representation: for each input word, the model selects a symbol to encode the word, and a role in which to place the symbol, and binds the two together. The selection is via soft attention. The overall interpretation is built from interpretations of the symbols, as recruited by the trained model, and interpretations of the roles as used by the model. We find support for our initial hypothesis that symbols can be interpreted as lexical-semantic word meanings, while roles can be interpreted as approximations of grammatical roles (or categories)such as subject, wh-word, determiner, etc. Fine-grained analysis reveals specific correspondences between the learned roles and parts of speech as assigned by a standard tagger(Toutanova et al. 2003), and finds several discrepancies in the model’s favor. In this sense, the model learns significant aspectsof grammar, after having been exposed solely to linguistically unannotated text, questions, and answers: no prior linguistic knowledge is given to the model. What is given is the means to build representations using symbols and roles, with an inductive bias favoring use of these in an approximately discrete manner.

papers.title: Calibrating Factual Knowledge in Pretrained Language Models
papers.research_question: How do we calibrate factual knowledge in Pretrained Language Models without re-training from scratch?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes CALINET, a lightweight method to calibrate factual knowledge in PLMs by adding and training new parameters (calibration memory slots) while freezing the original model, effectively reducing false knowledge and generalizing to downstream tasks.
papers.conclusion: The paper reassesses knowledge in PLMs with CKA, proposes CALINET to calibrate knowledge at scale without updating original parameters, and shows it generalizes well to downstream tasks, with neuron-level investigations into the calibration mechanism.
papers.key_findings:
Contrastive Knowledge Assessment (CKA) reveals that nearly 50% of facts are stored incorrectly in PLMs.
CALINET effectively calibrates false facts, reducing the False Rate from 48.10% to 17.09% for T5-base on 100 facts.
CALINET generalizes calibrated knowledge to downstream question answering tasks, improving performance on calibration subsets without harming performance on other questions.
Analysis shows that calibration memory slots are more knowledge-intensive than original FFN values, with nearly 80% corresponding to meaningful concepts.
CALINET adjusts the output token distribution to increase the probability of the correct fact and its synonyms, indicating generalized calibration.
papers.limitation:
Relies on existing knowledge bases and synthetic data for assessment and calibration, which may not fully capture real-world knowledge complexity.
Evaluates PLMs via their predictions, which is a biased approach and may not accurately assess factual knowledge correctness.
Cannot completely calibrate all factual errors in PLMs.
future_direction: Improve calibration applicability in reality by moving beyond synthetic data.
Develop more accurate methods for assessing factual knowledge correctness in PLMs.
Develop more advanced knowledge calibration methods.
papers.abstract: Previous literature has proved that Pretrained Language Models (PLMs) can store factual knowledge. However, we find that facts stored in the PLMs are not always correct. It motivates us to explore a fundamental question: How do we calibrate factual knowledge in PLMs without re-training from scratch? In this work, we propose a simple and lightweight method CaliNet to achieve this goal. To be specific, we first detect whether PLMs can learn the right facts via a contrastive score between right and fake facts. If not, we then use a lightweight method to add and adapt new parameters to specific factual texts. Experiments on the knowledge probing task show the calibration effectiveness and efficiency. In addition, through closed-book question answering, we find that the calibrated PLM possesses knowledge generalization ability after finetuning.Beyond the calibration performance, we further investigate and visualize the knowledge calibration mechanism.

papers.title: N-Gram Learning and Pretraining Dynamics in Transformer Language Models
papers.research_question: How do transformer language models acquire capabilities during pretraining, and what is the relationship between n-gram probabilities and this learning process?
papers.core_contribution: The dissertation demonstrates a close relationship between n-gram probabilities and language model learning during pretraining, showing that language model learning is highly dependent on surface-level statistics and identifies bigram subnetworks as a minimal circuit for next token prediction.
papers.conclusion: The results demonstrate a close relationship between n-gram probabilities and language model learning, suggesting that traditional distributional statistics still play a role in complex transformer models. Bigram subnetworks comprise a minimal subset of parameters necessary and sufficient for basic next token predictions.
papers.key_findings:
Language models learn words differently from human children; word frequencies (unigram probabilities) account for the vast majority of variance in words' ages of acquisition in language models, but not in children.
Language model learning can be characterized as early n-gram learning for increasing n, followed by gradual refinement of low-probability n-gram predictions based on longer contexts and more nuanced capabilities.
Subnetworks that make bigram predictions exist in fully trained language models and are critical for model performance, even when they consist of less than 0.2% of model parameters.
Bigram subnetworks are concentrated in the first Transformer MLP layer and overlap significantly with subnetworks trained to optimally prune a given model.
Bigram subnetworks recreate a pattern from the full models where the first layer induces a sharp change that aligns activations with next token predictions rather than current token representations.
papers.limitation:
Surprisal is an imperfect proxy for language model learning; a model might achieve the same surprisal at different points using different internal prediction strategies.
The work only considers language models with 124M parameters trained on 5.1B tokens, and learning curves may differ across model sizes.
future_direction: Further research is necessary to determine the effects of model size on learning speed, variability, and forgetting.
Characterize the examples (e.g., based on types of reasoning, world knowledge, or commonsense) that fluctuate at different points during pre-training across model sizes.
Bigram subnetworks can lay a foundation for studying more complex language model circuits by building up from a minimal circuit.
papers.abstract: Transformer language models have received unprecedented attention in recent years due to impressive performance on natural language tasks, but how they acquire these capabilities is largely unknown. During pretraining, language models are trained to predict next tokens (e.g. words) in text, and the field of pretraining dynamics aims to demonstrate how this learning objective leads to consistent learning patterns and mechanisms. The primary contributions of this dissertation are to demonstrate relationships between n-gram probabilities (next token predictions based only on the previous n-1 tokens) and language model learning during pretraining. I first show that language models learn words differently from human children; word frequencies (unigram probabilities) account for the vast majority of variance in words’ ages of acquisition in language models, but not in children. I then characterize language model learning as early n-gram learning for increasing n, then gradual refinement of low probability n-gram predictions based on longer contexts and more nuanced capabilities. Mechanistically, subnetworks that make bigram predictions exist in the models long after the full models have moved on from simple bigram predictions. These bigram subnetworks are critical to language modeling performance even in fully trained models, and they recreate several key properties of a language model’s activation space across layers. Together, these results demonstrate a close relationship between n-gram probabilities and language model learning, suggesting that traditional distributional statistics still play some role in these more complex models.

papers.title: Contextual Gradient Interference: A Novel Mechanism for Knowledge Retention and Adaptability in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How to mitigate catastrophic forgetting in large language models by enabling knowledge retention while adapting to new tasks through a gradient-based mechanism?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the Contextual Gradient Interference mechanism, a dual-gradient framework that dynamically partitions parameter updates to mitigate catastrophic forgetting and enhance knowledge retention and adaptability in large language models.
papers.conclusion: The Contextual Gradient Interference mechanism successfully addresses catastrophic forgetting by balancing knowledge preservation and task adaptation, demonstrating improved performance and scalability in large language models.
papers.key_findings:
The CGI mechanism improves accuracy, reduces perplexity, and enhances retention scores across various tasks.
It outperforms baseline models in retention scores for sequential learning tasks.
The model shows adaptability to variable contexts, though performance declines with increased complexity in multi-hop reasoning.
Scalability tests show accuracy plateaus beyond 100GB dataset size, with training time increasing non-linearly.
The model is robust to noisy inputs but accuracy decreases with higher noise levels.
papers.limitation:
Increased computational overhead associated with gradient decomposition and real-time masking
Reliance on auxiliary loss functions requiring careful hyperparameter calibration
Sensitivity to input quality under noisy conditions
future_direction: Investigating alternative methods for gradient decomposition, such as sparse or low-rank approximations
Incorporating reinforcement learning paradigms to dynamically adjust masking parameters based on task feedback
Exploring integration with emerging architectures, such as sparse attention or memory-augmented transformers
papers.abstract: Addressing the challenge of catastrophic forgetting in large-scale neural architectures requires innovative solutions that enable models to retain prior knowledge while adapting to new tasks. The proposed Contextual Gradient Interference mechanism introduces a dual-gradient framework designed to partition parameter updates dynamically, ensuring stability for previously learned information while facilitating effective task-specific adaptations. By leveraging real-time gradient analysis and masking strategies, the mechanism mitigates interference and promotes efficient learning across sequential tasks. The integration of this approach within the Falcon model, a state-of-the-art open-source language model, demonstrated significant improvements in knowledge retention, task adaptability, and robustness under varying conditions, including noisy inputs and increasing dataset sizes. Quantitative evaluations across multiple benchmarks revealed enhanced accuracy, lower perplexity, and improved memory retention compared to existing methodologies. The scalability of the approach was further validated through its computational efficiency and performance consistency over extended training cycles. Additional experiments highlighted the ability of the model to handle multi-hop reasoning and sequential tasks with complex contextual dependencies, showcasing the versatility of the proposed mechanism. An ablation study reinforced the significance of key components, such as gradient masking and decomposition, in achieving the observed performance gains. Results also revealed areas for potential optimization, including computational trade-offs and sensitivity to hyperparameter configurations. The study advances the understanding of gradient-based learning strategies and their critical role in optimizing neural networks for dynamic and large-scale tasks. Through its novel contributions, the mechanism establishes a foundation for enhancing the stability, adaptability, and efficiency of language model training, making it an invaluable tool for future developments in machine learning.

papers.title: A Language Model's Guide Through Latent Space
papers.research_question: To what degree do current concept detection and guidance strategies work for a richer set of concepts such as appropriateness, humor, creativity, and quality, beyond the previously studied truthfulness?
papers.core_contribution: Extends concept guidance to novel concepts like appropriateness, humor, creativity, and quality, finding that detectability does not always predict guidability, and introduces a novel metric (perplexity-normalized effect size) to evaluate guidance quality.
papers.conclusion: The work warrants a deeper investigation into the interplay between detectability, guidability, and the nature of the concept, and provides a rich experimental test-bed for guidance research.
papers.key_findings:
Truthfulness is robustly guidable with current techniques.
Novel concepts like humor need extensive tuning for successful guidance.
Appropriateness remains difficult to elicit and can lead to confusion with compliance.
Probes with optimal detection accuracies do not necessarily make for the optimal guides, contradicting previous observations for truthfulness.
papers.abstract: Concept guidance has emerged as a cheap and simple way to control the behavior of language models by probing their hidden representations for concept vectors and using them to perturb activations at inference time. While the focus of previous work has largely been on truthfulness, in this paper we extend this framework to a richer set of concepts such as appropriateness, humor, creativity and quality, and explore to what degree current detection and guidance strategies work in these challenging settings. To facilitate evaluation, we develop a novel metric for concept guidance that takes into account both the success of concept elicitation as well as the potential degradation in fluency of the guided model. Our extensive experiments reveal that while some concepts such as truthfulness more easily allow for guidance with current techniques, novel concepts such as appropriateness or humor either remain difficult to elicit, need extensive tuning to work, or even experience confusion. Moreover, we find that probes with optimal detection accuracies do not necessarily make for the optimal guides, contradicting previous observations for truthfulness. Our work warrants a deeper investigation into the interplay between detectability, guidability, and the nature of the concept, and we hope that our rich experimental test-bed for guidance research inspires stronger follow-up approaches.

papers.title: From Condensation to Rank Collapse: A Two-Stage Analysis of Transformer Training Dynamics
papers.research_question: This paper investigates whether the training dynamics of transformers can be analyzed independently of specific tasks, and specifically examines the dynamics under small initialization.
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides a two-stage theoretical framework for transformer training dynamics under small initialization, showing initial condensation of outer parameters followed by rank collapse of key-query matrices.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that transformer training dynamics under small initialization can be characterized by a two-stage process of condensation and rank collapse, which is supported by theoretical analysis and empirical evidence.
papers.key_findings:
Under small initialization, transformer parameters exhibit blow-up dynamics, escaping the small initialization regime in finite time.
During the first stage, outer parameters (WV, W^[1], W^[2]) undergo condensation, aligning row-wise toward a target direction.
After outer parameters reach a quasi-steady state, key-query matrices (WQ, WK) become active and their normalized versions undergo asymptotic rank collapse.
The two-stage dynamics (condensation followed by rank collapse) are theoretically proven and experimentally validated on synthetic and real datasets.
The analysis generalizes classical directional convergence results and offers a theoretical foundation for transformer optimization.
papers.abstract: Although transformer-based models have shown exceptional empirical performance, the fundamental principles governing their training dynamics are inadequately characterized beyond configuration-specific studies. Inspired by empirical evidence showing improved reasoning capabilities under small initialization scales in language models, we employ the gradient flow analytical framework established in [Zhou et al. NeurIPS 2022] to systematically investigate linearized Transformer training dynamics. Our theoretical analysis dissects the dynamics of attention modules into two distinct stages. In the first stage, asymmetric weight perturbations from random initialization sustain non-degenerate gradient dynamics in parameter matrices, facilitating systematic escape from small initialization regimes. Subsequently, these matrices undergo condensation, progressively aligning toward the target orientation. In the second stage, the previously static key-query matrices actively participate in training, driving the normalized matrices toward asymptotic rank collapse. This two-stage framework generalizes classical directional convergence results.

papers.title: BERTnesia: Investigating the capture and forgetting of knowledge in BERT
papers.research_question: How is relational knowledge distributed across BERT's layers, and how does fine-tuning affect the retention and forgetting of such knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a layerwise probing framework for BERT and finds that intermediate layers contain significant relational knowledge, which is forgotten during fine-tuning, with the extent of forgetting depending on the fine-tuning objective.
papers.conclusion: The proposed layerwise probing framework reveals that BERT stores significant knowledge in intermediate layers, which is forgotten during fine-tuning, with ranking tasks mitigating forgetting more than QA tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Intermediate layers contain a substantial amount of knowledge (17-60% of total knowledge) that is not present in the last layer.
Relational knowledge emerges at varying rates across layers, with some relation types doubling in the last layer and others being maximally captured in intermediate layers.
Fine-tuning causes forgetting of relational knowledge, but the amount of forgetting is influenced by the fine-tuning objective, not the dataset size.
Ranking models forget the least and retain more knowledge in their final layer compared to QA models.
The total knowledge in BERT is underestimated when only the last layer is probed.
papers.limitation:
Probing with cloze statements may conflate task-specific knowledge (masked word prediction) with factual knowledge, especially for MLM models.
Probes are limited to single-token factual knowledge, excluding multi-word entities and relations.
future_direction: Investigating ranking models with different training objectives (pointwise, pairwise, listwise).
Studying knowledge-intensive QA models like answer generation models.
Applying the framework to study variants of BERT architecture and pre-training methods.
papers.abstract: Probing complex language models has recently revealed several insights into linguistic and semantic patterns found in the learned representations. In this paper, we probe BERT specifically to understand and measure the relational knowledge it captures. We utilize knowledge base completion tasks to probe every layer of pre-trained as well as fine-tuned BERT (ranking, question answering, NER). Our findings show that knowledge is not just contained in BERT's final layers. Intermediate layers contribute a significant amount (17-60%) to the total knowledge found. Probing intermediate layers also reveals how different types of knowledge emerge at varying rates. When BERT is fine-tuned, relational knowledge is forgotten but the extent of forgetting is impacted by the fine-tuning objective but not the size of the dataset. We found that ranking models forget the least and retain more knowledge in their final layer. We release our code on github 1 to repeat the experiments.

papers.title: Cracking Factual Knowledge: A Comprehensive Analysis of Degenerate Knowledge Neurons in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How are degenerate knowledge neurons (DKNs) defined and acquired, and what is their relationship to the robustness, evolvability, and complexity of large language models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides a comprehensive definition of degenerate knowledge neurons (DKNs) from structural and functional perspectives and introduces the Neurological Topology Clustering method for accurate DKN acquisition, demonstrating that DKNs are linked to the robustness, evolvability, and complexity of large language models.
papers.conclusion: The paper provides a comprehensive definition of DKNs and introduces the neurological topology clustering method for precise DKN acquisition, and through extensive experiments demonstrates the critical role of DKNs in the robustness, evolvability, and complexity of PLMs.
papers.key_findings:
DKNs identified by the Neurological Topology Clustering method exhibit strong degeneracy, meaning suppressing a subset of Base Degenerate Components (BDCs) does not significantly affect prediction probability, while suppressing all BDCs does.
DKNs help PLMs cope with input interference, indicating their contribution to model robustness.
DKNs have strong fact-checking ability, outperforming knowledge neurons and direct PLM-based fact-checking.
PLMs utilize DKNs to learn new knowledge, as parameter changes during fine-tuning highly overlap with DKNs.
Efficient fine-tuning by freezing all MLP neurons except DKNs enables PLMs to learn new knowledge while preserving old knowledge, highlighting DKNs' role in evolvability.
papers.limitation:
Limited to GPT-2 and LLaMA2-7b models; validation on larger models is needed.
Confined to factual knowledge; applicability to other knowledge types is unknown.
Generalizability across different languages and cultural contexts is an open question due to the use of English datasets.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) store extensive factual knowledge, but the underlying mechanisms remain unclear. Previous research suggests that factual knowledge is stored within multi-layer perceptron weights, and some storage units exhibit degeneracy, referred to as Degenerate Knowledge Neurons (DKNs). Despite the novelty and unique properties of this concept, it has not been rigorously defined or systematically studied. We first consider the connection weight patterns of MLP neurons and define DKNs from both structural and functional aspects. Based on this, we introduce the Neurological Topology Clustering method, which allows the formation of DKNs in any numbers and structures, leading to a more accurate DKN acquisition. Furthermore, inspired by cognitive science, we explore the relationship between DKNs and the robustness, evolvability, and complexity of LLMs. Our execution of 34 experiments under 6 settings demonstrates the connection between DKNs and these three properties. The code will be available soon.

papers.title: ORCA: Interpreting Prompted Language Models via Locating Supporting Data Evidence in the Ocean of Pretraining Data
papers.research_question: From where does a pretrained language model learn task-specific knowledge in a zero-shot setup? Specifically, how can we locate a very small subset of pretraining data that directly supports the model in the task?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes ORCA, a method to locate a small subset of pretraining data (supporting data evidence) that directly influences a model's performance on a downstream task, and finds that BERT relies heavily on BookCorpus and pretraining examples masking task verbalizer synonyms.
papers.conclusion: ORCA can identify supporting data evidence in pretraining data for downstream tasks, and analysis of this evidence reveals BERT's heavy reliance on BookCorpus and pretraining examples that mask task verbalizers and synonyms.
papers.key_findings:
ORCA effectively identifies a small subset of pretraining data that, when used for continued pretraining, improves model performance on downstream tasks like sentiment analysis and textual entailment.
BERT shows a substantial reliance on BookCorpus, the smaller of its two pretraining corpora, for both sentiment analysis and textual entailment tasks.
A high percentage of masked tokens in the identified supporting data evidence are the task's verbalizer words (e.g., 'good', 'bad') or their synonyms.
The context of the supporting data evidence is not superficially similar to the task input data, as measured by MAUVE similarity, suggesting the useful signal is subtle.
papers.limitation:
The problem formulation ignores the history of model pretraining; a data point truly related to the task might have been overfitted in earlier stages, so continuing pretraining on it would not change the model.
ORCA is not guaranteed to find the global optimal supporting data evidence.
ORCA is slow and currently operates on only a small amount (0.5%) of the pretraining data due to computational constraints.
future_direction: Improving the theoretical grounding of the data evidence quality definition.
Extending ORCA to operate on the whole pretraining data and exploring potential design choices (e.g., warmup selections, annealing mechanisms).
Complementing high-level evidence analysis with more detailed interpretations (e.g., what exact spans in the supporting data evidence contribute to their supportiveness).
papers.abstract: Large pretrained language models have been performing increasingly well in a variety of downstream tasks via prompting. However, it remains unclear from where the model learns the task-specific knowledge, especially in a zero-shot setup. In this work, we want to find evidence of the model's task-specific competence from pretraining and are specifically interested in locating a very small subset of pretraining data that directly supports the model in the task. We call such a subset supporting data evidence and propose a novel method ORCA to effectively identify it, by iteratively using gradient information related to the downstream task. This supporting data evidence offers interesting insights about the prompted language models: in the tasks of sentiment analysis and textual entailment, BERT shows a substantial reliance on BookCorpus, the smaller corpus of BERT's two pretraining corpora, as well as on pretraining examples that mask out synonyms to the task verbalizers.

papers.title: Intrinsic Test of Unlearning Using Parametric Knowledge Traces
papers.research_question: How can unlearning methods be evaluated beyond behavioral tests by examining changes in parametric knowledge traces within model parameters?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a benchmark and intrinsic evaluation methodology for unlearning based on parametric concept vectors, showing current methods suppress but do not erase knowledge, and that erasing these vectors improves robustness.
papers.conclusion: Unlearning methods should be evaluated intrinsically by monitoring the erasure of parametric knowledge traces, and current methods largely fail to achieve this, highlighting the need for new approaches that effectively remove knowledge from model parameters.
papers.key_findings:
Existing unlearning methods introduce minimal changes to parametric concept vectors, mostly suppressing their activation at inference rather than erasing the knowledge.
Direct ablation (e.g., adding noise) of identified concept vectors effectively removes the associated knowledge and reduces the model's susceptibility to adversarial jailbreak attacks.
Jailbreak attacks can reactivate suppressed parametric knowledge by increasing the activation of concept vectors.
Behavioral evaluations alone are insufficient to assess unlearning; parameter-based intrinsic evaluations are necessary to verify knowledge erasure.
papers.limitation: The benchmark is non-exhaustive and may omit concepts for which no selective, causally significant concept vectors exist.
future_direction: Developing automated methods for creating large-scale benchmarks of parametric knowledge traces.
Further study on the existence and properties of selective concept vectors across different models and concepts.
papers.abstract: The task of "unlearning" certain concepts in large language models (LLMs) has attracted immense attention recently, due to its importance in mitigating undesirable model behaviours, such as the generation of harmful, private, or incorrect information. Current protocols to evaluate unlearning methods largely rely on behavioral tests, without monitoring the presence of unlearned knowledge within the model's parameters. This residual knowledge can be adversarially exploited to recover the erased information post-unlearning. We argue that unlearning should also be evaluated internally, by considering changes in the parametric knowledge traces of the unlearned concepts. To this end, we propose a general evaluation methodology that leverages vocabulary projections to inspect concepts encoded in model parameters. We use this approach to localize "concept vectors" - parameter vectors that encode concrete concepts - and construct ConceptVectors, a benchmark dataset containing hundreds of common concepts and their parametric knowledge traces within two open-source LLMs. Evaluation on ConceptVectors shows that existing unlearning methods minimally impact concept vectors and mostly suppress them during inference, while directly ablating these vectors demonstrably removes the associated knowledge and significantly reduces the model's susceptibility to adversarial manipulation. Our results highlight limitations in behavioral-based unlearning evaluations and call for future work to include parameter-based evaluations. To support this, we release our code and benchmark at https://github.com/yihuaihong/ConceptVectors.

papers.title: A Representation Level Analysis of NMT Model Robustness to Grammatical Errors
papers.research_question: How do NMT models represent and handle grammatical errors to achieve robustness? How does grammatical error representation differ across models and languages? How does fine-tuning for robustness influence models to achieve improved robustness?
papers.core_contribution: NMT encoders inherently implement a grammatical error correction setup by first detecting errors and then correcting them by moving representations towards correct forms. Fine-tuning for robustness enhances this process by increasing reliance on Robustness Heads.
papers.conclusion: The encoder implements a grammatical error correction setup for robustness, and fine-tuning only the encoder on noisy data can substantially improve robustness without degrading performance on clean data. The analysis framework combining GED probing, representational similarity, and Robustness Heads is model-agnostic and generalizable.
papers.key_findings:
GED probing performance increases in early encoder layers and plateaus or decreases in later layers, with noise-finetuned models showing degradation in deeper layers where correction occurs.
Representation distance between ungrammatical words and their correct forms generally decreases through encoder layers, especially in noise-finetuned models where similarity approaches zero.
Robustness Heads attend to interpretable POS tags relevant to the grammatical error type, such as nouns for article errors or verbs for preposition errors.
Fine-tuned models rely more on Robustness Heads for updating ungrammatical word representations, particularly in deeper layers, compared to base or clean-finetuned models.
Models respond similarly to grammatical errors across architectures, but representation differences exist across languages due to linguistic features.
papers.limitation:
All languages studied belong to the Indo-European family, which might limit generalization to other languages.
Synthetic noise is used, which may not fully simulate natural noise.
Focus on relatively small models due to resource limitations, while larger models might be more robust.
future_direction: Extend the analysis to decoder-only models.
Analyze the effects of different pre-training strategies and training data on robustness.
papers.abstract: Understanding robustness is essential for building reliable NLP systems. Unfortunately, in the context of machine translation, previous work mainly focused on documenting robustness failures or improving robustness. In contrast, we study robustness from a model representation perspective by looking at internal model representations of ungrammatical inputs and how they evolve through model layers. For this purpose, we perform Grammatical Error Detection (GED) probing and representational similarity analysis. Our findings indicate that the encoder first detects the grammatical error, then corrects it by moving its representation toward the correct form. To understand what contributes to this process, we turn to the attention mechanism where we identify what we term Robustness Heads. We find that Robustness Heads attend to interpretable linguistic units when responding to grammatical errors, and that when we fine-tune models for robustness, they tend to rely more on Robustness Heads for updating the ungrammatical word representation.

papers.title: Effects of Parameter Norm Growth During Transformer Training: Inductive Bias from Gradient Descent
papers.research_question: What are the effects of parameter norm growth during transformer training on the network's representations and inductive bias?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that parameter norm growth during transformer training leads to saturation, which characterizes an inductive bias of gradient descent and explains the emergent representations in attention heads.
papers.conclusion: The paper empirically found that parameter norm grows ∝ √t during T5 pretraining, likely due to approximate homogeneity, proved that norm growth induces saturation, and showed that pretrained transformers become approximately saturated, with attention heads splitting into argmax and mean behaviors.
papers.key_findings:
Parameter norm grows proportionally to √t during T5 pretraining.
Norm growth induces saturation, where the network approximates a discretized network with saturated activation functions.
Pretrained transformers (T5, XLNet, etc.) show high saturation levels compared to randomly initialized ones.
Saturated attention heads exhibit two types: argmax (attending to few positions) and mean (attending uniformly).
The dynamics of norm growth can be explained by approximate homogeneity of transformers and misaligned gradients.
papers.limitation: The theoretical analysis assumes uniform norm growth across all parameters, which may not always hold.
future_direction: Future works are encouraged to track norm growth metrics during pretraining of new transformer language models.
The investigation of the function of attention heads that lie between argmax and mean modes is deferred to future work.
Developing a more complete theoretical story for weight decay and norm growth is left for future work.
papers.abstract: The capacity of neural networks like the widely adopted transformer is known to be very high. Evidence is emerging that they learn successfully due to inductive bias in the training routine, typically a variant of gradient descent (GD). To better understand this bias, we study the tendency for transformer parameters to grow in magnitude ( 2 norm) during training, and its implications for the emergent representations within self attention layers. Empirically, we document norm growth in the training of transformer language models, including T5 during its pretraining. As the parameters grow in magnitude, we prove that the network approximates a discretized network with saturated activation functions. Such "saturated" networks are known to have a reduced capacity compared to the full network family that can be described in terms of formal languages and automata. Our results suggest saturation is a new characterization of an inductive bias implicit in GD of particular interest for NLP. We leverage the emergent discrete structure in a saturated transformer to analyze the role of different attention heads, finding that some focus locally on a small number of positions, while other heads compute global averages, allowing counting. We believe understanding the interplay between these two capabilities may shed further light on the structure of computation within large transformers.

papers.title: Debiasing NLU Models via Causal Intervention and Counterfactual Reasoning
papers.research_question: How to reduce biases in NLU models that arise from spurious correlations in training data using causal inference?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a debiasing framework for NLU models using causal intervention and counterfactual reasoning to remove spurious correlations and hypothesis-only bias.
papers.conclusion: The proposed causal inference-based debiasing strategy is effective and agnostic to the base encoder models.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed CICR framework outperforms previous debiasing methods on bias-sensitive datasets (SNLI-hard and FEVER symmetric test sets) by large margins.
The method maintains the original in-distribution performance on SNLI and FEVER datasets.
Ablation studies show that both causal intervention and counterfactual reasoning components are effective.
future_direction: Developing a more complex causal graph with external knowledge within the counterfactual inference framework.
papers.abstract: Recent studies have shown that strong Natural Language Understanding (NLU) models are prone to relying on annotation biases of the datasets as a shortcut, which goes against the underlying mechanisms of the task of interest. To reduce such biases, several recent works introduce debiasing methods to regularize the training process of targeted NLU models. In this paper, we provide a new perspective with causal inference to find out the bias. On one hand, we show that there is an unobserved confounder for the natural language utterances and their respective classes, leading to spurious correlations from training data. To remove such confounder, the backdoor adjustment with causal intervention is utilized to find the true causal effect, which makes the training process fundamentally different from the traditional likelihood estimation. On the other hand, in inference process, we formulate the bias as the direct causal effect and remove it by pursuing the indirect causal effect with counterfactual reasoning. We conduct experiments on large-scale natural language inference and fact verification benchmarks, evaluating on bias sensitive datasets that are specifically designed to assess the robustness of models against known biases in the training data. Experimental results show that our proposed debiasing framework outperforms previous state-of-the-art debiasing methods while maintaining the original in-distribution performance.

papers.title: Activation-Space Personality Steering: Hybrid Layer Selection for Stable Trait Control in LLMs
papers.research_question: How can we reliably control or align personality traits (Big Five) in Large Language Model generation through targeted interventions in the model's internal activations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a pipeline for personality steering in LLMs that extracts low-rank trait directions from activations and uses a hybrid (verified + dynamic) layer selection strategy to inject these directions into the residual stream, enabling precise control of Big Five trait expression without retraining.
papers.conclusion: The proposed activation-space personality steering framework with hybrid layer selection provides a robust and effective method for controlling personality traits in LLMs, bridging psychological theory and practical model alignment without degrading core capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
Personality traits in LLMs occupy a low-rank shared subspace, with top three principal components explaining over 90% of variance.
A hybrid layer selection strategy (combining offline verified layers and prompt-specific dynamic layers) yields stronger and more stable trait steering than using either component alone.
The steering method effectively shifts trait expression in both positive and negative directions while largely preserving the model's fluency and general reasoning capabilities (as measured by MMLU and ARC-Challenge).
The learned trait direction vectors exhibit structured correlations (e.g., between Openness and Extraversion), indicating shared representational structure for personality-related behaviors.
Steering effectiveness varies across model families, with some dependencies observed between traits when steered simultaneously.
papers.limitation:
Steering effectiveness is greater on some model families (e.g., Llama, Mistral) than others (e.g., Qwen).
Dependencies between traits (e.g., agreeableness and openness) can complicate independent steering, and applying orthogonality to remove these dependencies reduces steering efficacy.
The effect of steering is less significant when the base model's trait expression is already at an extreme (very high or very low).
future_direction: Disentangling trait-specific control from shared semantic structure without degrading steering effectiveness.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models exhibit implicit personalities in their generation, but reliably controlling or aligning these traits to meet specific needs remains an open challenge. The need for effective mechanisms for behavioural manipulation of the model during generation is a critical gap in the literature that needs to be fulfilled. Personality-aware LLMs hold a promising direction towards this objective. However, the relationship between these psychological constructs and their representations within LLMs remains underexplored and requires further investigation. Moreover, it is intriguing to understand and study the use of these representations to steer the models' behaviour. We propose a novel pipeline that extracts hidden state activations from transformer layers using the Big Five Personality Traits (Openness, Conscientiousness, Extraversion, Agreeableness and Neuroticism), which is a comprehensive and empirically validated framework to model human personality applies low-rank subspace discovery methods, and identifies trait-specific optimal layers across different model architectures for robust injection. The resulting personality-aligned directions are then operationalised through a flexible steering framework with dynamic layer selection, enabling precise control of trait expression in LLM outputs. Our findings reveal that personality traits occupy a low-rank shared subspace, and that these latent structures can be transformed into actionable mechanisms for effective steering through careful perturbations without impacting the fluency, variance and general capabilities, helping to bridge the gap between psychological theory and practical model alignment.

papers.title: Editing Models with Task Arithmetic
papers.research_question: How can we steer the behavior of neural networks by performing arithmetic operations on task vectors (weight differences between fine-tuned and pre-trained models)?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces task vectors and shows that simple arithmetic operations (negation, addition, analogy) on them can effectively edit model behavior for forgetting, multi-task learning, and task analogies.
papers.conclusion: Task arithmetic is a simple, efficient, and effective way to edit models.
papers.key_findings:
Negating a task vector reduces performance on the target task with little change in control tasks.
Adding task vectors from multiple tasks creates a single multi-task model competitive with multiple specialized models.
Task analogies (e.g., A:B::C:D) allow improving performance on a task with no data by combining vectors from three related tasks.
Task vectors from different tasks are nearly orthogonal, enabling combination without interference.
The method is simple, efficient, and effective across models, modalities, and tasks.
papers.limitation: Task vectors are restricted to models with the same architecture and require the same pre-trained initialization.
future_direction: Exploring merging only shared weights when fine-tuning introduces new parameters (like a new head).
Using more sophisticated strategies for scaling coefficients.
Relaxing the assumption of same pre-trained initialization.
papers.abstract: Changing how pre-trained models behave -- e.g., improving their performance on a downstream task or mitigating biases learned during pre-training -- is a common practice when developing machine learning systems. In this work, we propose a new paradigm for steering the behavior of neural networks, centered around \textit{task vectors}. A task vector specifies a direction in the weight space of a pre-trained model, such that movement in that direction improves performance on the task. We build task vectors by subtracting the weights of a pre-trained model from the weights of the same model after fine-tuning on a task. We show that these task vectors can be modified and combined together through arithmetic operations such as negation and addition, and the behavior of the resulting model is steered accordingly. Negating a task vector decreases performance on the target task, with little change in model behavior on control tasks. Moreover, adding task vectors together can improve performance on multiple tasks at once. Finally, when tasks are linked by an analogy relationship of the form ``A is to B as C is to D", combining task vectors from three of the tasks can improve performance on the fourth, even when no data from the fourth task is used for training. Overall, our experiments with several models, modalities and tasks show that task arithmetic is a simple, efficient and effective way of editing models.

papers.title: From Emergence to Control: Probing and Modulating Self-Reflection in Language Models
papers.abstract: Self-reflection -- the ability of a large language model (LLM) to revisit, evaluate, and revise its own reasoning -- has recently emerged as a powerful behavior enabled by reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR). While self-reflection correlates with improved reasoning accuracy, its origin and underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood. In this work, {\it we first show that self-reflection is not exclusive to RLVR fine-tuned models: it already emerges, albeit rarely, in pretrained models}. To probe this latent ability, we introduce Reflection-Inducing Probing, a method that injects reflection-triggering reasoning traces from fine-tuned models into pretrained models. This intervention raises self-reflection frequency of Qwen2.5 from 0.6\% to 18.6\%, revealing a hidden capacity for reflection. Moreover, our analysis of internal representations shows that both pretrained and fine-tuned models maintain hidden states that distinctly separate self-reflective from non-reflective contexts. Leveraging this observation, {\it we then construct a self-reflection vector, a direction in activation space associated with self-reflective reasoning}. By manipulating this vector, we enable bidirectional control over the self-reflective behavior for both pretrained and fine-tuned models. Experiments across multiple reasoning benchmarks show that enhancing these vectors improves reasoning performance by up to 12\%, while suppressing them reduces computational cost, providing a flexible mechanism to navigate the trade-off between reasoning quality and efficiency without requiring additional training. Our findings further our understanding of self-reflection and support a growing body of work showing that understanding model internals can enable precise behavioral control.

papers.title: Memory-Based Model Editing at Scale
papers.research_question: How can we design a model editor that accurately models an edit's intended scope and handles many edits without failure, overcoming the limitations of existing gradient-based editors?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SERAC, a memory-based model editing method that uses a scope classifier and counterfactual model to accurately update model behavior without modifying base model parameters, achieving high performance on challenging editing problems.
papers.conclusion: SERAC provides a high-performance, efficient, and reusable solution for model editing, effectively handling challenging edit scopes and multiple edits.
papers.key_findings:
SERAC achieves higher edit success and lower drawdown than existing methods on multiple editing problems.
SERAC maintains performance when applying many edits, while other methods degrade.
SERAC's editor can be reused across different base models without retraining.
Cross-attention scope classifier improves performance on fact-checking tasks.
papers.limitation: The ability to modulate a model's opinions or beliefs about any topic has profound impacts on model governance and could be misused, e.g., for propaganda.
papers.abstract: Even the largest neural networks make errors, and once-correct predictions can become invalid as the world changes. Model editors make local updates to the behavior of base (pre-trained) models to inject updated knowledge or correct undesirable behaviors. Existing model editors have shown promise, but also suffer from insufficient expressiveness: they struggle to accurately model an edit's intended scope (examples affected by the edit), leading to inaccurate predictions for test inputs loosely related to the edit, and they often fail altogether after many edits. As a higher-capacity alternative, we propose Semi-Parametric Editing with a Retrieval-Augmented Counterfactual Model (SERAC), which stores edits in an explicit memory and learns to reason over them to modulate the base model's predictions as needed. To enable more rigorous evaluation of model editors, we introduce three challenging language model editing problems based on question answering, fact-checking, and dialogue generation. We find that only SERAC achieves high performance on all three problems, consistently outperforming existing approaches to model editing by a significant margin. Code, data, and additional project information will be made available at https://sites.google.com/view/serac-editing.

papers.title: Physics of Language Models: Part 3.1, Knowledge Storage and Extraction
papers.research_question: How do language models memorize knowledge during training, and extract it later to answer questions or perform logical reasoning during inference?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that knowledge augmentation (e.g., paraphrasing, sentence shuffling) in pretraining data is crucial for reliable knowledge extraction via instruction fine-tuning, and introduces linear probing techniques to explain this phenomenon.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes with practical recommendations for LLM pretraining: data rewriting (augmentation) is important, and including instruction-like data in pretraining is beneficial.
papers.key_findings:
Mixed training (pretraining on both biographies and QA data) enables knowledge extraction, but the model learns in an abnormal way (first from QA then correlates with BIO).
Without knowledge augmentation in pretraining, instruction fine-tuning fails to extract knowledge (0% accuracy).
Knowledge augmentation (e.g., paraphrasing, sentence shuffling, translations) during pretraining enables knowledge extraction after fine-tuning.
Linear probing shows that knowledge augmentation causes knowledge to be linearly encoded in the hidden embeddings of entity names, whereas without augmentation it is distributed across tokens.
Including celebrity data (with augmentation) in pretraining improves knowledge extraction for minority data (without augmentation).
future_direction: Studying logical reasoning and knowledge manipulation
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can store a vast amount of world knowledge, often extractable via question-answering (e.g., "What is Abraham Lincoln's birthday?"). However, do they answer such questions based on exposure to similar questions during training (i.e., cheating), or by genuinely learning to extract knowledge from sources like Wikipedia? In this paper, we investigate this issue using a controlled biography dataset. We find a strong correlation between the model's ability to extract knowledge and various diversity measures of the training data. $\textbf{Essentially}$, for knowledge to be reliably extracted, it must be sufficiently augmented (e.g., through paraphrasing, sentence shuffling, translations) $\textit{during pretraining}$. Without such augmentation, knowledge may be memorized but not extractable, leading to 0% accuracy, regardless of subsequent instruction fine-tuning. To understand why this occurs, we employ (nearly) linear probing to demonstrate a strong connection between the observed correlation and how the model internally encodes knowledge -- whether it is linearly encoded in the hidden embeddings of entity names or distributed across other token embeddings in the training text. This paper provides $\textbf{several key recommendations for LLM pretraining in the industry}$: (1) rewrite the pretraining data -- using small, auxiliary models -- to provide knowledge augmentation, and (2) incorporate more instruction-finetuning data into the pretraining stage before it becomes too late.

papers.title: What does it mean to be language-agnostic? Probing multilingual sentence encoders for typological properties
papers.research_question: How do multilingual sentence encoders capture typological properties of languages, and how does this vary with different pretraining strategies?
papers.core_contribution: Multilingual sentence encoders capture typological properties, but the encoding differs based on pretraining objectives: models with cross-lingual objectives (LASER, XLM) lose typological information in higher layers and create a shared interlingual space, while models with monolingual objectives (M-BERT, XLM-R) retain typological information in all layers and partition the space into language-specific subspaces.
papers.conclusion: There is a trade-off between universality and language-specific information in multilingual encoders, and pretraining objectives influence how typological information is encoded.
papers.key_findings:
All encoders capture some typological properties (word order, pronouns, negation).
M-BERT and XLM-R outperform LASER and XLM on lexical and morphological properties.
Typological information is localizable in lower layers of LASER and XLM, but spread across all layers in M-BERT and XLM-R.
Cross-lingual training leads to more language-agnostic representations but at the cost of losing language-specific typological information in higher layers.
XLM generalizes to languages unseen during pretraining, capturing their typological properties.
papers.abstract: Multilingual sentence encoders have seen much success in cross-lingual model transfer for downstream NLP tasks. Yet, we know relatively little about the properties of individual languages or the general patterns of linguistic variation that they encode. We propose methods for probing sentence representations from state-of-the-art multilingual encoders (LASER, M-BERT, XLM and XLM-R) with respect to a range of typological properties pertaining to lexical, morphological and syntactic structure. In addition, we investigate how this information is distributed across all layers of the models. Our results show interesting differences in encoding linguistic variation associated with different pretraining strategies.

papers.title: LLM Knowledge is Brittle: Truthfulness Representations Rely on Superficial Resemblance
papers.research_question: Do LLMs learn robust underlying knowledge representations, or are they fragile and tied to the exact phrasings and formulations seen during training?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs' internal representations of statement truthfulness are brittle and degrade under superficial, semantically-preserving transformations, indicating that knowledge representations rely on superficial resemblance to pre-training data rather than robust, generalizable knowledge.
papers.conclusion: LLMs learn shallow, non-robust knowledge representations that fail to generalize to scenarios unlike those seen during training, presenting a fundamental challenge for the utility of truthfulness probes and the reliability of LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Truthfulness separability degrades as samples become more out-of-distribution (OOD) across all probing methods, datasets, and model families.
Certain topics (e.g., sociology, marketing) have more robust representations than others (e.g., history).
Benchmark performance does not imply robust representations; knowledge representations degrade even for questions the model answers correctly.
Larger models may not be more robust; the 70B Llama model showed the steepest degradation in some cases.
The type of transformation affects degradation differently; translation breaks representations while negation does not affect internal probe performance.
papers.limitation:
Analysis limited to decoder-only autoregressive language models.
Use of perplexity as a proxy for out-of-distribution (OOD) may not be perfect.
Only semantically-preserving transformations are considered.
future_direction: Improving the robustness of learned knowledge representations.
Extending the analysis to other model architectures (e.g., encoder-decoder models).
Exploring other types of distribution shifts beyond superficial transformations.
papers.abstract: For Large Language Models (LLMs) to be reliable, they must learn robust knowledge that can be generally applied in diverse settings -- often unlike those seen during training. Yet, extensive research has shown that LLM performance can be brittle, with models exhibiting excessive sensitivity to trivial input variations. In this work, we explore whether this brittleness is a direct result of unstable internal knowledge representations. To explore this question, we build on previous work showing that LLM representations encode statement truthfulness -- i.e., true, factual statements can be easily separated from false, inaccurate ones. Specifically, we test the robustness of learned knowledge by evaluating representation separability on samples that have undergone superficial transformations to drive them out-of-distribution (OOD), such as typos or reformulations. By applying semantically-preserving perturbations, we study how separability degrades as statements become more OOD, across four LLM families, five evaluation datasets, and three knowledge probing methods. Our results reveal that internal representations of statement truthfulness collapse as the samples' presentations become less similar to those seen during pre-training. While LLMs can often distinguish between true and false statements when they closely resemble the pre-training data, this ability is highly dependent on the statement's exact surface form. These findings offer a possible explanation for brittle benchmark performance: LLMs may learn shallow, non-robust knowledge representations that allow for only limited generalizability. Our work presents a fundamental challenge for the utility of truthfulness probes, and more broadly, calls for further research on improving the robustness of learned knowledge representations.

papers.title: Probing Linguistic Features of Sentence-Level Representations in Relation Extraction
papers.research_question: What linguistic features are captured by sentence-level representations in neural relation extraction models, and how do different encoder architectures and the inclusion of linguistic features affect the learned representations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a set of 14 probing tasks specifically designed for relation extraction and uses them to analyze how encoder architectures and linguistic features bias the linguistic properties captured in sentence-level representations.
papers.conclusion: The paper introduces probing tasks for relation extraction and shows that encoder architectures and linguistic features bias the learned representations, with self-attentive encoders capturing deeper features not fully captured by the probing tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Adding contextualized word representations (ELMo, BERT) greatly increases performance on probing tasks focusing on named entity and part-of-speech information, and yields better results in relation extraction.
Entity masking improves relation extraction performance but considerably lowers performance on entity type related probing tasks, indicating a shift in focus away from entity mentions.
Encoder architecture bias clearly affects learned properties: CNN and Bi-LSTM perform well on local probing tasks (e.g., argument distance, part-of-speech context), while GCN performs well on dependency-related tasks.
Self-attentive encoders show superior relation extraction performance but consistently perform lower on the probing tasks, suggesting they capture 'deeper' linguistic features not covered by the current probing tasks.
Probing task performance does not necessarily correlate with relation extraction performance; models that perform better on probing tasks do not always perform better on the downstream task.
papers.limitation: The probing tasks do not cover all linguistic patterns, such as appositions, and do not investigate generalization to specific entity types.
future_direction: Extend the probing tasks to cover specific linguistic patterns such as appositions.
Investigate a model's ability of generalizing to specific entity types, e.g., company and person names.
papers.abstract: Despite the recent progress, little is known about the features captured by state-of-the-art neural relation extraction (RE) models. Common methods encode the source sentence, conditioned on the entity mentions, before classifying the relation. However, the complexity of the task makes it difficult to understand how encoder architecture and supporting linguistic knowledge affect the features learned by the encoder.
